subsubtopic: INCREASED TAX BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition on behalf of a number of petitioners who believe that the tax burden on average families is roughly $1,000 greater than it was in 1984. They point out that millions of dollars have been taken from Canadian families through Government cuts to benefit programs. They also point out that one in six Canadian children is living in poverty.
Therefore, the petitioners are asking Parliament to provide tax relief and fairness to Canadian families and ask that it considers the advisability of increasing benefits paid through the family allowance and the refundable child tax credit.

subtopic: PETITIONS
subsubtopic: EQUAL PAY AND OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, another group of petitioners are concerned that women working
full-time earn on average only 66 per cent of what men earn and that more than 18 per cent of women working full time and almost 79 per cent of those employed on a part-time basis earn less than $10,000. They point out that only 22 per cent of women employed full time earn $25,000 annually or more. They list a set of other concerns in terms of the bias against women in the workplace. They call upon Parliament to introduce and systematically enforce legislation guaranteeing Canadian women equal pay for work of equal value and equal opportunity for employment.

subtopic: PETITIONS
subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF PETRO-CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour today to present a petition on behalf of a number of Canadians in which they argue that the Government of Canada has failed to take measures to remove Canadian petroleum assets from foreign control. They further point out that the Government of Canada has weakened its ability to ensure that Canadian gas and oil is developed in the national interest. On the basis of these two factors, they petition Parliament to ensure that 100 per cent of the ownership of Petro-Canada remains in the hands of the Government of Canada.

speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-3, an Act to establish the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, to repeal the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion Act and to make consequential amendments to to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and on the amendment of Mr. Langdon:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
This House declines to give second reading to Bill C-3 because it fails to clearly define federal government responsibility for regional development, and specifically fails to reflect the requirement under s. 36(l)(b) of the Constitution Act, 1982, that Parliament is committed to "furthering economic development to reduce disparity in opportunities".

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate, a debate on a Bill to create a new Department of Industry, Science and Technology. Throughout the next few minutes I would like to bring forward a western point of view.
I want to to point out strongly that I do not want to sound parochial in this matter. After all, westerners, and particularly the good people in my province, feel that they are Canadians first, that they have a lot of faith in this country. We do have in our part of the country some very special concerns. I believe that these concerns must be addressed, and they ought to be addressed in this particular debate. I will touch on some of these concerns as we go along.
We recognize the crucial need to strengthen the economy, particularly in the regions. One way to increase the strength of the economy is to increase our commitment to research and development. In my opinion, that should be at the very top of our list. In an age of technology, research and development ought to be a top priority. One way of doing that is by providing adequate funding, not just bureaucratic shuffling. That is what we see in this particular Bill, bureaucratic shuffling, no real commitment to R and D. I believe this is consistent with this Government's record. I want to point out that since 1984 there has been an appalling neglect of R and D funding.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made some pretty big promises in this regard. For example, he promised a doubling of research and development spending in the first four years of the first mandate of the Government. The Prime Minister did not keep that promise. I want to point out one particular fact. As a percentage of Gross Domestic Product, R and D spending slipped from 1.37 per cent to 1.35 per cent. So much for promises. So much for commitment to managing change in this country.
This is something I want to point out because it was stressed very heavily by the Conservative Party in the last election campaign. We all remember what the Prime Minister said. He said that it was his Party that was best equipped to manage change. How do we manage change in Canada? One way we do that is by staying on the leading edge of technology. It is central to economic growth. It is central to productivity. What have we received from the Government in this regard? We certainly have received promises, shrinking commitment to R and D. We have received bureaucratic games, shuffling people around, creating new positions, renaming Departments. That is not very impressive.
From a western perspective, there are a number of concerns that we have. The western economy, as most people understand, is based on resources and agriculture. That kind of an economy is at the mercy of external forces. We can do almost nothing about these external forces. There are many factors that come into this picture. For example, commodity prices can go up and down in just a matter of minutes. There is the ever present threat of a drought. We had one in the West last year, and it could happen again this year. Oil prices can go up and down at just about a moment's notice. We in the West are always in a rather precarious situation. We need to diversify. We have to give our economy more legs on which to stand. That is why industrial, scientific and technological development is most crucial to the West.
April 25, 1989

Adding to our concerns is the fact that our existing industries, ones that are there already, have been hit by a spate of recent mergers. I would like to mention a couple of them. One is the Molson merger. The other is the purchase of Wardair by PWA. These consolidations have led to fewer jobs. To make matters even worse for our region, high tech firms in the West have closed. Some of them have moved to eastern Canada. I believe that the Government has to take some responsibility in this regard. We have to point out the Government's lack of commitment in the encouragement of secondary industry in the West. That has to be told to the Canadian public.
The Government is weak in this area of encouraging secondary industry in the West. Instead of encouraging development of secondary industry in our region, the policies of the Government appear to have the opposite effect. They appear to have the effect of centralizing industry in central Canada. Instead of recognizing the importance of regional development, instead of developing policies to spur regional development, what do we get? We get bureaucratic shuffling and the renaming of Departments. That is not good enough.
The Government wants to create a Department which would be the focus of developing industrial policies. Fair enough. This particular Bill does not mention the West or what the role of the Department of Western Diversification will be. It does not specify what the role will be of that particular Department. That raises concerns in our minds. We must ask what will be the benefit of this new Department of Industry, Science and Technology to the West. What will be the benefit to our region? We fear that the concerns of the West will be overlooked. We fear this because the mandate for economic development in the West falls outside of the scope of this new Department, outside of its particular mandate. We fear that the economic development of the West will somehow become peripheral and secondary to that of central Canada. It is significant that only the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec are mentioned in this legislation. Our information is that the focus of industrial development will be fixed in central Canada and that the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology will institutionalize that focus.
Industry, Science and Technology
How then will the West fit in? That is the question. Can the Department of Western Economic Diversification deliver? Can it really get for the West the West's fair share? Will the Minister of that particular Department have the stature and the clout to ensure that the West gets its fair share?
There is another question. We consider this one crucial. The spending authority of the Department of Western Economic Diversification ends in just three years' time, in just 36 months. What happens then? Will we be left out in the cold? That is a real fear. That is exactly what has happened to the ERDA agreements. They have been left to wither on the vine.
We need to know the future of the Western Diversification Office. If it loses its spending authority, who then is left to pick up the pieces?
The Government could dismiss these concerns as just so much political talk, but these concerns are very real. We already know the Government's track record. We know of its insensitivity to regional development, particularly in my home province of Manitoba. We know what has happened to the ERDA agreements.
I would like to single out the ERDA agreements because in the recent past they have been a cornerstone of regional economic development. They were even recognized by the Prime Minister in an October 3, 1986 speech when he described the agreements as historic. Perhaps, instead, he should have said that they were history.
These agreements ought to be renegotiated. They should be renegotiated. We consider that the time to do that is now. The time is crucial. If the provinces want to renegotiate the agreements and they are ready to renegotiate, then why is the federal Government not ready?
I want to remind the House of something that was said by the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne). He said: "It was the Progressive Conservative Government that was not afraid to sit down with the provinces and see what, exactly, they wanted". So why now at this particular time is the Government suddenly afraid to sit down with the provinces calmly and with a spirit of co-operation to renegotiate these agreements with the provinces? I suggest that if the Government wants to be taken seriously on this particular matter, it should be prepared to do so, and to do so right now.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
The then Minister for International Trade in 1985 made one of those statements that often comes back to haunt him. He said: "The ERDAs would continue at the current rate of spending". I think that commitment was about as real as the Government's commitment to the UI system. The ERDA agreements were particularly important to my Province of Manitoba and were used in many projects such as reforestation, transportation, mineral and agri-food development. The ERDA agreements were good for the province, good for the region, good for our people, and are needed more than ever right now because of the difficult economic times that we face.
There is another matter which I consider particularly relevant in this debate, the matter of federal procurement in our region and in my province, for the Government has not delivered to the Province of Manitoba. It has not come through. Statistics on this issue are revealing.
While Manitoba is ranked fifth in terms of population with 4.2 per cent of the country's total population, my province's share of federal Government contracts is below 3 per cent. It is distressing to note that while a quarter of federal procurement in 1986-87 was for items valued in excess of $50 million, Manitoba did not get one contract worth that much. That does not do anything for western alienation.
There was an interesting article in the Winnipeg Free Press the past weekend. There are revelations in the article that I believe should be inserted into the House of Commons record. I want to refer specifically to the article in the Winnipeg Free Press where that particular newspaper looked at federal and provincial spending records and estimates, Statistics Canada summaries of transfer payments and federal employment, Government records of supply and services purchases, and a province-by-province breakdown of spending through Ottawa's Western Diversification Office. These are some of the findings by the Winnipeg Free Press.
First, the Manitoba Government received an estimated $10.58 of every $1,000 Ottawa spent in the year ending March 31, 1989, compared to $10.74 spent in the year ending March 31, 1984. That was the last full year of Liberal Government in this country.
Now that may not sound like very much but if Ottawa had continued, according to the Winnipeg Free Press article, giving the same share of total spending to the provincial Government, the Manitoba treasury would have received an added $307 million over the past five years. Three hundred and seven million dollars to a province like Manitoba is a lot of money.
Second, employment in Manitoba dropped by 2,446 people between October, 1984, and March, 1988, as Ottawa slashed the number of civil servants nation-wide. In Manitoba, the cut in the yearly federal payroll is about $71 million at today's average rate of pay. Seventy-one million dollars is not chicken feed to a small province like Manitoba.
Third, Manitoba municipalities have suffered as Ottawa cut support for local Governments through the country. Between 1984 and 1987, which is the last year of complete figures, average federal support for Manitoba municipalities dropped by 2.9 per cent or $600,000 a year, a significant contribution to the municipalities of the Province of Manitoba.
Fourth, Manitoba's share of federal supply and services purchases dropped to 2.84 per cent in 1987, compared with an average of 3.3 per cent during the eight years before the Prime Minister took office. That drop cost Manitoba suppliers $93 million In government business during the past three years, which is not chicken feed.
There is one more point that I want to raise that was contained in the Winnipeg Free Press article over the weekend. Per capita funding for Manitoba-based projects through the Western Diversification Office stood at $40 by April 7 compared to $43 in Alberta, $77 in British Columbia, and $118 in Saskatchewan. Manitoba would have received $28 million more had its share of funding corresponded to Manitoba's share of western Canada's population. Lamentably, those figures point out that my Province of Manitoba is not getting its fair share. All Manitoba has always asked for is its fair share.

Industry, Science and Technology

Member recognizes this reference undoubtedly stems from the fact that we have the excellent programs that the Government has put in place in the area of western economic diversification. Does the Hon. Member seriously think that the Party which forms the Government, which enjoys and has for so many years enjoyed the support of western Canadians, would forget for one minute to safeguard the economic development interests of western Canada, not to mention Atlantic Canada?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my hon. friend. I suppose that his question is rhetorical. He asks whether the Government would abandon the West. On the surface one would say that, surely, it would not be good politics to abandon the West. However, the fact is that we have been shocked in the past. We have to be ready for almost anything that comes our way, particularly when it might represent or be tantamount to a punch in the nose.
My hon. friend may not remember that I represent the riding of Winnipeg-St. James. The people of Winnipeg-St. James will not forget for a long time what the Government did in terms of the CF-18 affair. We thought that we had won a contract. We thought that the Government had a commitment to the tendering process. We thought that the Government would not use politics and interfere with that time-honoured process. However, it did. A company in my riding, in my city, won a very rich contract fair and square. Yet the Government through sheer politics, through nothing more than a bid to garner votes in another province, interfered with that process and took that contract away from us. That was terrible. We are not going to forget it for a long time.
When the Hon. Member asks will the Government ever forget about the West, will it ever abandon the West, the answer is: "Yes, the Government will do that". We will not have short memories.
The Hon. Member also has to remember this. Perhaps he was not listening as closely as he should have been. The mandate of the Western Diversification Office will run out, according to legislation, in three years. What

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
will happen after that? That is a responsible question on our part. It is a concern that we have. Who knows, the Government could just wind down and then what will happen? We have a legitimate concern.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would just like to make a comment by way of responding in part not only to what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Harvard) said but also to what the Member across the way said about western Canada.
There is a tendency in this House, and I have seen it ever since I came here in 1979, to talk about western Canada as if it is some sort of homogeneous lump that does not have debates within itself about what is the appropriate policy for western Canada. I recall at the time of the National Energy Program when people would get up to say: "Western Canada is against the National Energy Program" when there were many western Canadians who were for the National Energy Program. Western Canada came to be identified in the Tory minds with the boardrooms of Calgary, Alberta.
The point I want to make is that western Canadians have delivered the Conservatives a message. It is that there are almost 40 members of Parliament not from the Government side who come from western Canada. There are some 19 New Democrats from B.C., 10 New Democrats from Saskatchewan, one New Democrat from Alberta, two New Democrats from Manitoba, five Liberals from Manitoba and one Liberal from B.C. The Hon. Member pretends that the Government has some kind of monopoly on western Canada. The fact is that the Conservatives were almost shut out of Winnipeg. For him to try to refute the thesis that western Canadians, in particular Winnipegers, were not particularly offended by the CF-18 decision, is the height of folly as far as I am concerned. People were offended. They showed that on November 21, 1988 by returning record numbers of non-Conservatives to the House of Commons from western Canada.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make the following comment, if you allow me.
I think that this Government in no way claims to have a monopoly on what should be done for regional development in Canada-in the West, the Maritimes or elsewhere.
As proof, unlike the previous Government, which had the habit of defining all regional development policies and procedures centrally, this Government has in fact decentralized, created advisory boards with people in the regions and reestablished the dialogue with the provincial governments; the regional policies have come out of consultations and cooperation with the local community.
Certainly, one can always do more for regional development. What this Government is trying to do by way of regional development policies with local people is to set long-term policies and strategies supported by local people so that everyone works together developing the economy. This approach yields results. Just look at the lower rates of unemployment and increased income.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise in this Chamber to engage in the debate on Bill C-3 which creates a new Department of Science and Industry from the old Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. In addition to the creation of a Minister of Science and a focus on science, there is the concern of this Party
April 25, 1989

with respect to this Department's responsibilities for regional development. Others of my colleagues will consider the deficiencies in that aspect of the Bill which limits this new Department's regional development responsibilities to Ontario and Quebec.
However, even with regard to those aspects which are favourable to its science and technology function, I find it extremely difficult to understand how it is going to be possible to integrate the science policy and regional development policy aspects of this new Department's responsibilities. There is a clear necessity for balanced development of science policy throughout the country if it is going to be appropriately integrated into industrial and economic growth. I hope that Members on the government side will address those questions, and perhaps some of my colleagues, in looking at the regional development aspect, will themselves consider it.
From the point of view of those of us who are very much concerned about the lack of an appropriate focus on research and development in this country, the creation of this new Department is a step forward. We certainly welcome a Minister of Science with a higher profile who will begin to accord the kind of recognition to science, research and development that we need. It certainly is an improvement over the old Minister of State status which was practically no status at all.
In contemplating what alternative actions might have been taken to bring about this increased profile to science to ensure that the Government gets proper advice, that there is within the government bureaucracy a commitment to the development of a science, research and development policy, one might have considered the alternative suggested by many of those preoccupied with basic research in universities, that a Department of Science, Research and Post-Secondary Education might have been created. This would have at least recognized the important role that universities play, not only with respect to providing the basic and fundamental research underpinning for any research enterprise in the country but also the critical role that post-secondary institutions are going to play in respect to providing the manpower, the scientists and the technicians that are going to be necessary for future growth.
Industry, Science and Technology
I am saying this in the context of a situation evolving in this country where we are suffering a severe shortage of trained personnel in those areas. Put another way, we are in a situation where not enough opportunity is being provided to young people who wish to become scientists. We are not providing enough appropriate support to the scientists we have to ensure that they will stay, either as scientists or as university teachers.
We are going to be facing a period in the 1990s when we are going to be suffering a severe shortage of university research scientists. We are not providing them through the pipeline of the universities. Since the United States is going to be facing the same problem, we are going to be facing a severe competitive situation in that respect.
I would have to concede, however, that a concept of a science and university or a research and university linkage in the designation of that kind of Department would be well taken. On the other hand, we could have had a free-standing Department of Science, Research and Development. We could have had a Minister who was quite independent of any other Minister, one who could have been equally able to address industrial and economic needs as well as the question of post-secondary institutions, basic research and so on. We could have had a Minister who accorded the kind of weight and importance to basic and fundamental research policies that most of us who understand science realize are necessary in order to ensure that we will have a viable scientific climate in this country. Basic research, if it is not there, is going to cost us dearly in the future.
I do not think that there is any compelling reason for opposing the Bill because we do not have a free-standing Department of Science, Research and Development, but one which is linked with industry. That is as acceptable as any other alternative except that one must worry about the bias which has been so frequently expressed by this Government which seems to disregard the role of basic research, which seems to disregard the role of the universities in ensuring that Canada has a viable research and development climate. We cannot borrow the findings of basic and fundamental research from other countries.
When I express this concern about this bias, it is not something that I draw from the air. The former Minister of DRIE said on a number of occasions that that science will be supported by a government which accords with

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
industrial priorities. It was said over and over again that science which is identified by politicians as being capable of generating industrial growth of new products in a relatively short time is the science that would be supported. This is expressed in a number of quite concrete ways. The granting councils, which are supposed to supply the essential funding to the universities for basic fundamental research, have not in the last several years received any significant increase in funding except that which accrues to them through the matching grants. It is strictly in the area of science by virtue of a granting program according to which moneys provided by industries to the universities will be matched by grants from the granting councils, which in turn will go to the universities. The bias is clear.
There is nothing inherently wrong with ensuring greater co-operation between the universities and industries in respect of research and development. There is something wrong and we have a serious problem when recommendations are ignored such as that made by the Lortie Commission-which derives from the National Advisory Council on Science and Technology, which advises the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)-that the amount of money provided to the granting councils should be doubled over two years, and thereafter increases to those granting councils be 1.5 times the increases the Gross National Product.
Scientists who understand the role of basic research recommend that the Government take certain actions, but the Government has failed to do so. Again, we must caution that the twinning of science with industry will not so bias our emphasis as to cloud our minds, as the Tory minds are already clouded with respect to the role of basic research. The Government has not done especially well even with respect to its primary concern with basic research. Let me cite another example in this respect.
One of the flagships of government policy has been the new centres of excellence. I believe the centres of excellence reflect a step forward in a number of respects, but when one considers the criteria to be applied in the selection of which centres of excellence will be funded, overwhelmingly the criteria are those which correspond to direct industrial, relatively short-term needs. If the Government evinced an appreciation of the appropriate role of basic research in order to give some balance to this, the centres of excellence would also have criteria
that would have been applicable to basic research emphasis in some centres of excellence.
Let us examine what this may entail. I suppose there is not a Member in the House who is not aware of the excitement being generated in the scientific community over fusion research. I was shocked to read in the Toronto Star last week that for some months Canadian scientists at Electrofuel, a small laboratory in Toronto, were working on cold fusion and had generated perhaps some 15 patents and may even have beat the Utah investigators except for the fact that they were inadequately funded. This tells me that whatever might be the outcome of the scientific interaction to occur with respect to coal fusion in terms of its mechanism, it is an example of research that bureaucrats or even eminent scientists cannot identify as an area of appropriate emphasis.
In the past I have cited the instance of genetic engineering, in which no one I know would have given significant funds to research on snake venom, snail juice or bacterial viruses. Yet those are areas which have led to great breakthroughs in genetic engineering. We must ensure that Canada is not deprived of those possibilities inherent in basic research.
The Government has not even done its job with respect to its preoccupation with industrial and applied research. The extent of this failure was dramatized only in the last few days by the revelation that Connaught Laboratories, a great historical institution in this country which derives from the discovery of insulin in Canada, is to be sold to Merieux of France. At the same time, Lumonics, one of the most advanced and third largest laser technology firms in the world will be sold to Sumitomo. One of the interesting aspects of Lumonics is that it is part of a centre of excellence in Ontario. It challenges one's imagination to come to grips with this small fact, but in Ontario there is a centre for advanced laser and lightwave research which is funded by the Government of Ontario. Government funding provided the laser technology in the first place. Lumonics is being funded as part of a centre of excellence in Ontario. The federal Government, and now the provincial Government, contributed to the technological development of this place. Now it will be sold.
If the Government is going to come to grips with research and development policy, surely one elementary, fundamental premise must be that when the technology and R and D in this country are developed here and funded by this country, they must be owned in this
April 25, 1989

country. Yet this self-evident, elementary fact of research and development policy is not minimally recognized by the Government or Investment Canada. I have no doubt that it does not even ask the question.
It is not the first time that we have lost technology that was developed here. If we are to go beyond the empty promises of the Prime Minister, then this new Department had better come to grips with those elements of appropriate research and development policy that are necessary to increase the rate of expenditure from the present 1.35 per cent of GNP to the level maintained by other industrial nations, which is about 2.5 per cent. Sweden is approaching 3 per cent of Gross National Product in this area.
The twinning of science and industry in this Department at least calls attention to the absolutely critical requirement to place strong emphasis on the area of creation of new knowledge and new products if we are to get beyond our resource dependency.
I repeat, ownership is fundamental. What has the Government done? It signed a deal with the United States so that any of the companies in this country worth less than $150 million, those companies which do most of the basic industrial research and development, can be bought by Americans without even a review, and take our research and development, take our technology, and take our jobs back to the United States.
If Lumonics and Connaught had available to them some funding from the federal Government, or some federal mechanism to obtain the funding in order to pursue their markets and expand their technologies themselves rather than selling out to foreigners to do it, we could have saved Connaught and Lumonics. However, no such mechanism exists.
According to the subsidy rules to which the Government will almost surely agree with the United States under the Free Trade Agreement, we will not be able to be selective in ensuring that Canadian companies are getting the funding to develop the technology that is necessary for their survival and for the new products we will need in order to be competitive.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the objectives of Bill C-3 as listed in Clauses 7, 10 and 12 are laudable indeed. However, I am deeply concerned that this Bill, which puts the crucial areas of science and technology within the same Department as industry, might conveniently allow the Government to over-em-phasize industrial issues and ignore the pressing need to increase expenditure in research and development, as it has ignored this need for the past four and a half years.
If the Government does not improve research and development policies, Canadians risk becoming technologically backward in a world of rapidly unfolding technological innovation. If more research funds are not devoted to science and technology we risk becoming permanently relegated to the kindergarten of science.
My concern is shared by many prominent scientists and economists, such as Polanyi and de Grandpre.
The consequences of continued neglect of research and development by the Government are grave. Canada will be unable to compete in the world market and our standard of living will falter. Given the link between economic and social policies, Canada's social programs will also suffer.
In my reply to the Speech from the Throne I discussed my Party's commitment to our universal social programs. Now I wish to focus on the Government's lack of commitment to research and development in science. May I remind the Government that we need more than a legislative Bill on paper; we need a Government with a will to act.
I am concerned that the new Department that will be created by Bill C-3 will not adequately reflect the necessary link between continued success in industry and greater devotion of resources to research and development which will allow us to create the technology to become more competitive on the international economic scene.
My concern has a genuine basis. In the last four and a half years the Government has not fulfilled its promises in the areas of science and technology. Further, the Government's current obsession with reducing the deficit may cause it to neglect funding of research and development.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Federal expenditure on research and development decreased 7 per cent from 1984 to 1988. In 1984 the Government promised to increase spending on research and development to 2.5 per cent of the Gross National Product before the end of its first mandate. However, funding actually decreased in real terms during this period. To use the words of the Hon. Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Andre), this is an example of the Government "saying one thing and acting in another way."
Does the Government know and appreciate the difference between a promise and a commitment? The Government has capped the base budgets of Canada's principal research and granting councils. It has also limited tax credits to companies conducting research.
As if the onslaught on research and development was not serious enough, the Government also drastically cut the budget of the National Research Council. Has the Government forgotten that the National Research Council is Canada's national laboratory and the primary research and development organization of the federal Government?
Instead of increasing the National Research Council's budget by 20 per cent, as the Government had promised, it did the exact opposite. It chopped the budget by 20 per cent. These cuts not only cause lay-offs, but they demonstrated the Government's lack of crucial foresight in developing Canada's future technology.
The Government tax credit system has been plagued by inefficiency and delay. Some prolonged delays, as long as 18 months in the processing of claims, have seriously hindered genuine research efforts. Small companies are hit hardest by such delays. They are forced to restrict their research and development programs because they lack the necessary capital to wait for the decision of the Government.
Members of the House will be the first to admit that the Government's record on research and development is abysmal. I might add that neglecting research and development exacerbates Canada's debt problem, since our inability to compete effectively in the world market will increase our deficit in the long run. The Government does not seem to realize the extremely serious state of Canada's research and development efforts.
Canada was last of eight major countries in total research and development spending. In 1987 total research and development in Canada was approximately 1.4 per cent of Gross Domestic Product, about half that of the United States and Japan. Canada was last in company-funded research and development, with only 3 per cent of Canadian firms investing in any research and development at all. Canada is last in the number of scientists and engineers that we have, which is less than 10 per thousand. It is no comfort that Canada was fourth in government-performed research and development as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product.
Such statistics are frightening when one realizes that science and technology have a greater role than ever before in determining economic prosperity. The research and development efforts in other countries together with the rapidity of technological changes are posing major challenges to the international competitiveness of Canadian industries.
Since research and development is a significant creator of jobs and wealth, the Government's low spending in this area is alarming indeed. Mr. Fraser, President of the Canadian Institute of Advanced Research said:
We have failed to understand that we are ill equipped to survive in a global economy based increasingly on science and technology-based products.
This lack of understanding is reflected by the fact that this Government has no clear policy on how to promote research. Public policy is essential in promoting and financing Canada's relatively small high-tech industry. Because of the huge investment required and the long wait for profits to materialize, the free market alone cannot be relied upon to finance research. There is a need for more joint industry-govemment-unversity research and development. Two hundred and forty million dollars to centres of excellence is not enough. I worry that the Government's words are not matched with dollars.
It is absolutely necessary for the Canadian Government to increase spending in the area of research and development. Not only must the Government increase direct support of research and development through larger grants to universities and through better scholarship programs for students, for example, but the Government must provide better successful, loop-hole free investment incentives so that private companies will also increase their research and development spending.
April 25, 1989

I am also concerned that the Government is not taking enough account of public opinion on the need to increase research and development spending. In 1987, the Ministry of State for Science and Technology found that 80 per cent of Canadians would like to see more development of science and technology. This Government has failed to take into account that public opinion. The public believes that Government should take the lead in this area and share the costs with the private sector and, I emphasize, with the provinces. My Province of Manitoba asks for no less than a fair share of federal support.
The public is also receptive to efforts to improve Canada's scientific capability, to keep scientists and technologists in Canada and to train more of them. Yet the Government has not taken the wishes or the best interests of Canadians into consideration when it decided its spending policy in the areas of research and science. This is one more classic example of this Government's pachydermous insensitivity to the Canadian scientific community!
Canada does not produce enough people with advanced degrees in natural science and engineering. There is a brain-drain of scientists due to the inefficient financing of education and research in Canadian universities. The Liberal Party supports the recommendations of the Lortie Commission. In some research and development areas in high-growth industries the demand for highly qualified human resources exceeds the supply. In the area of basic, as opposed to applied, research, the Government has been even less encouraging toward its human resources. This is alarming as well for without basic science the application of new knowledge is difficult. Yet Canada's support for university research is among the lowest in the major industrial countries on a per capita basis. As a percentage of Gross Domestic Product the funding of research in universities and granting councils is less today than it was in 1970.
This is unacceptable. As Nobel Prize winner, Dr. Gerhard Herzberg points out, it can be historically demonstrated that the truly revolutionary discoveries have come from individuals of great merit pursuing a relatively unfettered path. This Government's research and development program, to the extent that it has one, reflects the Government's preoccupation with profit that takes precedence over concerns about our scientists making progress in the area of basic science.
Industry, Science and Technology
I submit, Madam Speaker, that investment in research and development should be made on the basis of the common good not on the basis of political expediency. Many Canadian scientists and teachers of science predict that unless more support is given to basic research Canadian universities will lose their stars, those people most likely to make major scientific breakthroughs. Promising scholars may also be steered away from basic research after deciding that there is no career to be had in science in Canada. Indeed, I am concerned that the Government will not do enough to promote both applied and basic research in universities, to encourage industry in Canada to increase research and development activity and to foster their research and development in renewable technologies which are essential to implementing environmental improvement.
I also have some concerns with some specific clauses in Bill C-3, which I will mention only briefly here, but which must be examined carefully at the committee stage. First, I question whether the Minister of this new integrated department will be so preoccupied with industry, market-forces and and profit that he or she will not devote full equal attention to research, science and technology and that the result of the creation of this new integrated department may just be a camouflage which will make it look like the Government plans to address the need to increase research and development while really just allowing the Government to continue stalling in this area.
Second, I worry whether the Minister for Science will act in concurrence with the chief Minister as specified in Clause 4(3) but will not be subject to such control by the chief Minister that the Science Minister is unable to act independently and is instead only a puppet in promoting the needs of science.
Third, I would like to be assured that any recommendations made by the chief science adviser who will be appointed by the Governor in Council under Clause 5(3) will be taken into serious consideration by the Government and not ignored.
Fourth, I am concerned that including the issue of regional development of Ontario and Quebec within the responsibilities of this new department and leaving the regional development of other provinces and territories to other provincial-federal arrangements may lead to an unfair regional allocation of research and development funds. Manitoba and other provinces and territories would not ask that Ontario and Quebec receive less funding for research. We in the West only demand that

April 25. 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
all regions receive their fair share and are not sacrificed by the federal Government. Any imbalance in regional development is not only unfair, it is unethical.
In conclusion, I wish to ask the assurance of this Government that it will, for once, make an honest effort to stop ignoring the need to push for more research and development for all parts of this country and to lend credence to its words by taking some effective action.
If this Bill passes let it be a redeeming document which will reflect the Canadian commitment to fairness and ethics. Finally, if this Bill passes I hope that the Government will recognize with deeds and not just words the importance of increasing research and development which will allow us to sustain our national pride in our scientific achievements and maintain our economic prosperity which, in turn, will enable us to promote social justice in the form of providing social nets in the areas of unemployment, health and welfare.
The last four years were abysmal for the scientific and technological community as a consequence of neglect by the Government. The Liberal Party is committed to call this Government to task in scientific research to ensure that the next four years will undo the neglect of the past four years.

It speaks in words that would lead us to believe that in fact this Government is going to do something toward science, industry, technology, research and education.
I went back to the prior Bill which this Bill is repealing, the Regional Expansion Act. I looked through that Bill to find what was being changed, what we could look forward to in Government attitude from what was in the prior Bill. I found many of the same words in that Bill as are in this: develop, implement and promote international policies and entrepreneurship. Many of those are words that have been transplanted from that Bill into this Bill.
The Government must do more than talk in platitudes. It must do more than simply set down in words in a Bill what it will do. It must show through action what will happen under this administration. If it could not do it under the former Bill, it does not appear that, without the will and without the drive that is required, it is going to be able to do anything further with this Bill.
For instance, in the matter of research and development, we see that the thrust of this Bill is for increased research, increased development. I would suggest that one goes hand in hand with the other, and hand in hand with education, yet since 1984-1 think the figures will prove this-in fact the commitment of this Government to research has dropped substantially.
I was flipping through a position paper from the National Consortium of Scientific and Educational Societies and found some comments that I would like to read into the record.
On one page it states:
The concern of the member institutions of the National Consortium of Scientific and Education Societies of Canada is both with university education and research. The links between the health of these two economically essential sectors are obvious, and should be. Without productive, high quality undergraduate education, we cannot produce the right kind or number of graduate students. Without the right kind
and number of graduate students, the research enterprise will wither. Without research and development, no modern economy can assure or maintain for its citizens an acceptable standard of living - that Canada is seriously underinvesting in research and development. Also any attempt to raise the share of research and development in the national economy must be accompanied by a considerable increase in educated and trained researchers.
I suggest that the Government, while paying lip service to the research community, has been gutting that very institution. We have seen massive cut-backs for the past four and a half years in the area of research and in the area of development. That to us on this side of the House is unacceptable.
In my riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt we have an establishment, the Summerland Research Station for agriculture, which is an institution well respected around the world, not just in Canada. It is a magnificent facility built some years back with the capabilities, with the adequate funding, of doing something in the area of agriculture, for which the Okanagan is famous. Yet within that facility we have major research funding caps.
From my point of view I am pleased to see science, technology, and research coupled with small business. Certainly, in the agricultural area in my region one goes hand in hand with the other. Agriculture, after all, is a small business. The research done in the Summerland Research Station works with the agricultural community in taking fruit products and assisting those small businesses in developing by-products, what we know here and throughout Canada as value-added products. It is a small example of the value of research.
I would suggest to the House that for every dollar that we invest in the research community in the education of our young people and in maintaining that research community, we get back dividends far in excess not just for this generation but for generations of the future. Those dollars, whether they be for research in the agricultural area, the astrophysical area, the area of geriatric research or for medical research, will return dollars. However, we must provide those dollars to our scientific researchers in order that they can spread their wings and make these break-throughs and developments that will lead, in the future, to the cuts that we will be able to make in medical areas. The research that will be done will take away the necessity, perhaps, of so many trips of our aged and aging population to the doctors, the clinics, and the hospitals, thereby repaying a dividend in that area.
April 25, 1989

I would like to move on the area of small business. I have read Clause 8. On the surface it is laudable and applaudable. Using this Bill, the Minister will be able to strengthen the national economy, increase the international competitiveness of Canadian industry, encourage the fullest and most efficient and effective development and use of science and technology and develop, implement and promote national policies to foster an improvement in productivity and efficiency in industry. He will be able to develop and implement national policies to foster entrepreneurship and to start up growth and expansion of small business and promote and expand tourism. These thrusts are applaudable. However, I would suggest that they must be more than just words.
Small business in Canada since 1980 has created, according to Statistics Canada, just over 70 per cent of our new jobs. I suggest that of the approximately 800,000 small businesses in Canada, the small business persons are the economic backbone of our country. We in this House should do more than simply pay lip service, simply give out the usual platitudes. We should be bending over backward to assist small business, whether it be through financial assistance, assistance through the Federal Business Development Bank, assistance through our chartered banks, assistance through interest rates, or assistance through technology. We must do more for the small business community.
It was interesting in looking through the annual report of the Federal Business Development Bank and analysing some of the figures in it to find that in terms of the loans which it grants, over 82 per cent were over the $100,000 mark. The balance under that mark illustrates to some extent that the small business community is not gaining benefit from the Federal Business Development Bank. In going through facts and figures from small business, we find that 85 per cent of small business loans are made through chartered banks. It is interesting to note the problems that small businesses have in dealing with chartered banks. One of the largest complaints is that they are required to put up collateral much in excess of what would normally be required and much in excess of the loan that they are receiving. For each dollar of loan that a small business in Canada takes from a chartered bank, it must put up in collateral $2.78 worth of assets.
Industry, Science and Technology
Small businesses are also overburdened with the paperwork required in order to process many of these loans. Mountains of paperwork is involved. They have to deal with matters such as secured loans, mortgages, chattel mortgages, assignment of book debts, and the list goes on. Since most small businesses employ under five people, it is the business person who has to deal with this paperwork. He has to deal with the lawyers and the accountants in order to help them. Therefore, his overhead goes up. It is in this area that the Government could be cutting down on some of the red tape. It should be cutting down on some of the paperwork required. In this way he or she will have the opportunity to pursue their assistance to the economy with the aim of being able to put bread and butter on their tables.
On the surface the thrust of this Bill appears to be laudable. However, there is an unfortunate quirk in it about which everyone in Canada should be made aware. It has been pointed out in the House before. This Bill leaves the economic development across Canada in the hands of three different Ministers. Instead of pulling it all together under the auspices of one ministry, it is spread out among three. If it were pulled together under one, there would be a unified thrust. We must have unity in Canada. We must show unity. We must not have separate ministries for the West, the East or for central Canada. Economics, research and development and technology must be dealt with even-handedly throughout all the provinces and all the regions of Canada.
Unfortunately, this Bill leaves the way open for regional disparities to crop up and cause problems for the generation of the future. Instead of bringing forward a unified Bill which would bring the regions together, the Government appears to be dividing the country into three areas. They are the Atlantic, the West and central Canada. Over the years we have watched the growing disparities between the eastern provinces and central Canada and between the western provinces and central Canada. One of the arguments that we hear constantly on the doorsteps and the streets of our ridings is that we in the West are not receiving our fair share. I am sure the same is true with respect to the East. We need equality with the rest of Canada, a unified Canada that Sir John A. Macdonald worked so hard to bring together. We need a Government that will bring in policies to unify and govern with an even hand regardless of how the electorate voted in the last election or how it is perceived that it will vote in the next.

April 25, 1989
There are a number of areas in the Bill at which I think the Government should look. In terms of British Columbia and the West, the lumber industry is one of those areas. It can use some of that research and development assistance to create value-added products. Instead of shipping our lumber and logs raw, we should be looking at methods to add value to them. This would assist the people and entrepreneurs in the regions to use what we are producing in our sawmills and pulp mills, in the creation of products that would stimulate the number of jobs in Canada for Canadians, products not only for consumption in Canada but for consumption abroad. If Canada is to survive and thrive in the economics of today's world, we can no longer be hewers of wood and drawers of water. We must progress. We must do it with fervour and with one goal in mind. We must reach that goal. However, we cannot achieve it without the funding and the backing of the Government.
The unemployment rate in my region is enormous. It is over twice the national average. This is an area in which value-added products in agriculture, forestry and mining could add to the employment base.
I suggest that in the future the Government put the Federal Business Development Bank back into the business of making small entrepreneurs its first priority. I suggest the Government reduce the unnecessary forms and red tape and target federal contracts to the small business sector. I suggest the Government establish a more aggressive "buy Canada" program and an export marketing agency to help small manufacturers with limited resources to make contacts abroad. I suggest that the Government prohibit banks from requiring small businesses to meet unreasonable collateral requirements on loans. There should be a push from the Government for a commitment from the banks to stop discriminating against women who seek start-up loans.
Those are some of the suggestions that I put forward. I ask that the Government listen to them in the future before it puts this Bill into law.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Quebec Environment Minister Lise Bacon should immediately remove the PCBs in Quebec schools and hospitals and store them safely in the regions they come from, not send them to Senneterre in Abitibi-Temiscamingue. speechtext:

They gathered to consider a proposal which would have New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and P.E.I. form a legislative union. To this meeting came five officials from Canada, John A. Macdonald, Georges Etienne Cartier, George Brown, Alexander Galt and Thomas D'Arcy McGee. They came, as an historian of the time stated:
April 25, 1989

To till the fertile soil of reason and to plant the seeds of a great nation.

subtopic: FUND-RAISING IN UNIONVILLE, ONTARIO
FUND-RAISING IN UNIONVILLE, ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last fall two and a half year-old Jeffrey Savage of Unionville was hit by a car and became a paraplegic. His mother, Deb, brought Jeffrey home from the hospital this month. The entire proceeds of the Unionville Village Festival dance in June will go towards Jeffrey's care and rehabilitation as he starts down a new and difficult path.
Earlier this year, 18 year-old Kurt Gengenbach of Unionville suffered a severe spinal injury in a hockey accident. Next week on May 4, over 1,200 people will be attending a fund-raising dinner for Kurt at $100 a plate. On May 7, a "Run for Kurt" will take place starting at Unionville High School. Proceeds from both these events will go toward Kurt's home care and renovations to his home for wheelchair accessibility.
I salute and applaud all those people of my riding of Markham who are participating in these warm and generous expressions of goodwill.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED NATIONAL SALES TAX
IMPACT OF PROPOSED NATIONAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Finance Minister's statement yesterday
that he will act alone without the assistance of the provinces to implement his pet project, a new national sales tax, indicates the futility of that exercise, and like his equally unmoving determination on interest rates, shows how out of step with Canadians he is on the economy.
Canadians do not want high interest rates and they do not want the new national sales tax program which threatens everything from new home construction, as argued by the Canadian Real Estate Association, to our children's music education.
This Government is continuing to fail to protect Canadian interests. The Free Trade Agreement, high interest rates and the value of the dollar are killing the small manufacturer. At the same time the proposed national sales tax will cripple the consumer. What we need in this country is a real tax reform and a Minister of Finance who understands the Canadian economy and the needs of the ordinary Canadian citizen.

subtopic: PLIGHT OF SALLY ESPINELLI
PLIGHT OF SALLY ESPINELLI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, three months ago the Minister of Employment and Immigration allowed Violeta Juayong to remain in Canada. Sally Espineli, also of my community, was not so fortunate. She was deported eight months ago on the same grounds as Violeta, that she misrepresented her marital status.
Late last week the Canadian Human Rights Commission ruled that discrimination may have occurred in her case. The agony for Sally, and for many others who entered Winnipeg under similar conditions, have continued. I now urge the Minister to show the same humanitarian concern for Sally Espineli, and bring her back to Canada now instead of waiting for the final decision of the Human Rights Tribunal.
My sentiments are shared by all members of my community, by the Premier of Manitoba, by members of the Opposition and also by senior members of the Cabinet and government caucus. I am confident the Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will do the right and honourable thing and promptly end the human suffering of my community by taking action to rectify this intolerable situation.

April 25, 1989

subtopic: ENUMERATION PROVISIONS OF URBAN AND RURAL DWELLERS
ENUMERATION PROVISIONS OF URBAN AND RURAL DWELLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the enumeration leading up to the last federal election, many of my constituents were out of town when enumeration took place. There were some people who were in the riding who were not enumerated and for that reason they lost the right to vote. It seems ironic that federal judges and lately the mentally handicapped have won the right to vote from a federal judge, yet urban dwellers such as those in my riding of Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold remained out in the cold.
Rural dwellers can register to vote right up to voting time, but urban dwellers must do so by the seventeenth day before the elections. I think that this is unfair. I believe that urban voters should be able to register to vote right up to election day just like rural people and that way they will not be disenfranchised.
Mr. Arthur Mills of my riding was one of the disenfranchised Canadians. On his behalf and on behalf of Canadians who did not have a chance to vote, I urge that the Government address this problem and correct it before the next federal election.

subtopic: UTILIZATION OF WESTERN CANADIAN LOW-SULPHUR COAL URGED
UTILIZATION OF WESTERN CANADIAN LOW-SULPHUR COAL URGED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to encourage the Government of Canada to do all that is necessary and practical to encourage the utilization of western Canada low-sulphur coal in the central Canadian industrial basin. The western coal would largely displace imported coal from Pennsylvania and elsewhere offshore. The implementation of this recommendation would accomplish two worthy objectives: First, by encouraging the use of a domestically produced coal, our nation's balance of payments would be improved. More important, because western Canada produces coal much lower in sulphur content, the subsequent emissions from the use of western coal is significantly preferred in protecting our environment from the contaminations of sulphur dioxide or acid rain. This suggestion could save Canada $2.4 billion, generate 13,000 permanent jobs and at the same time protect our soil, water and air from contamination.

subtopic: UNFAIR INCREASE IN TAXATION RATES ALLEGED
UNFAIR INCREASE IN TAXATION RATES ALLEGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I received a letter from a very troubled resident of Vavenby, British Columbia, who feels he has been excessively taxed. In 1986 on an income of $19,500 he paid $1,035 in income tax. However, by 1988 on an income of $23,000 he was forced to pay nearly $3,000 tax. In three years, while his income increased by 18 per cent, the Conservative Government increased his income tax by 175 per cent. He believes he has been unduly taxed. An $1,800 income tax grab from a man who has worked all his life for his community and his country is not right, especially when he knows that 60,000 large profitable corporations pay no taxes at all. This man from Vavenby,
April 25, 1989

British Columbia, whose income tax increased 175 per cent in three years says not that only will he not pay more income tax, he cannot pay more income tax. What will he say when he learns on Thursday that he soon will be forced to pay a new national sales tax for the purchase of clothing, books, car repairs, everything? I suggest that a taxpayer's revolt is in the making.

IMPORTANCE OF CHALLENGE '89 FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that my first statement in this Second Session of the 34th Parliament is good news for the young people in my riding.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, with the approval of 131 Challenge '89 projects in Quebec-Est, I am proud to announce that 238 students this summer will be able to benefit from a quality well-paying work experience, thanks to a federal financial contribution of $293,639.

subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF JET SERVICE TO STEPHENVILLE, NEWFOUNDLAND
DISCONTINUANCE OF JET SERVICE TO STEPHENVILLE, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Air Canada's plan to discontinue jet air service into Stephenville is an absolutely devastating body blow to the economy of southwestern Newfoundland.
Of course the move is a direct consequence of the Government's airline deregulation policy, a policy which decrees that the public's right to an adequate transportation network must play second fiddle to the whims and balance sheets of corporations.
It is a policy which is rapidly translating into inferior air service for people in less populated areas; a policy which, together with rural postal closings and railway abandonments,' is working wonders in the Government's grand scheme to shut down rural Canada.
There is just one way that Air Canada and its service to Stephenville can be saved, that is through the direct intervention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. B. Bouchard). His colleague, the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), already asked him to instruct the National Transportation Agency to hold public hearings on the matter. I now ask the Minister to do exactly that, with a view to according Newfoundland special designation as the NTA Act provides.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is National Secretaries' Day and I want to encourage everyone who works with a secretary to take a few moments to consider their value.
I suggest that every Member of the House and every manager in the country assess his or her effectiveness and recognize the contribution that their assistant or secretary has made toward that effectiveness. Receptionists, clerks and secretaries are seldom given the credit or respect they deserve. Yet they are as responsible as anyone for the continued efficient operation of our industrial plants, hospitals, businesses and offices.
Florists and restaurants will do well tomorrow as people recognize National Secretaries' Day, but I would encourage those buying the flowers and lunches to recognize also the importance of the position and the person who fills it.

LACK OF FUNDS
speechtext:

April 25, 1989

subtopic: TREATY FOR BANNING CHEMICAL WEAPONS PROPOSED
TREATY FOR BANNING CHEMICAL WEAPONS PROPOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the revelation that poison gas of some kind was used, fatally, against demonstrators in Georgia is very sorry news indeed. It must be widely condemned as totally reprehensible and never repeated again. Those who made the decision to use it should be brought to justice.
Unfortunately, it seems that the world is on a slippery slope to increased use and increased tolerance of chemical warfare, as we learned to our horror when Iraq employed chemical warfare on his Kurdish population in surely one of the most despicable acts in recent history.
There has been much talk of the need for a treaty to ban all such chemical weapons, as well there should be. It is certainly needed, not just to prevent nations from using such chemicals against each other but also to protect their own citizens. We urge the Government to actively promote such a treaty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise today, it is not lightheartedly; it is after deep reflection. I rise on a point of privilege.
To start I would like to quote from the House of Commons Office of the Law Clerk and Parliamentary Counsel the definition of privilege. The official definition of privilege is found in Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice:
Parliamentary privilege is the sum of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and by members of each House individually, without which they could not discharge their functions, and which exceed those possessed by other bodies or individuals. Thus privilege, though part of the law of the land, is to a certain extent an exemption from the ordinaty law.
I will deal specifically with breaches of privilege, the one of obstructing, molesting, or attempting to intimidate a Member in the discharge of his or her duties as it relates directly to me. I quote again from the December, 1988, Parliamentary Privileges Booklet, page 15, line 21:
Direct threats, however, whether oral or written, made to a Member on account of his or her actual or intended parliamentary conduct is a contempt of Parliament.
My complaint relates to threats or intimidation by another Member of this House on April 11, 1989 in the afternoon of that same day, by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes).
I want to put it in chronological order.
On April 5 the first draft of Standing Committees was given to Conservative Members. I had requested and was put on the Committee of Health and Welfare.
On April 11 the Conservative Members of that committee had an organizational meeting, which I attended. In the afternoon of that same day I was approached by my honourable colleague, the Member from Calgary West, and we had what he described as a friendly chat.
During that conversation he made it clear that he was not happy with my voting record in the Thirty-third Parliament and therefore could not trust me as long as I had this independent attitude. He threatened and told me he would take me off the committee unless I gave him a commitment to behave as a good boy, and if I would change my attitude he would reconsider and put me back on the committee and I would again be in his good graces. This friendly chat that took place can be confirmed by other Members.
Another means of intimidation was undertaken through the circulation of lists with names of Members who abstain on votes. The circulation of this list creates caucus peer pressure and in this way becomes a subtle form of intimidation.
I quote again from the December 8 Parliamentary Privileges Booklet. On page 15 it states:
Direct threats, however, whether oral or written, made to a
Member on account of his or her actual or intended parliamentary
conduct, is a contempt of Parliament.
The intimidation was done in two forms: one directly by threatening me to change my voting record, and indirectly it was done by publishing my name in pamphlets that were distributed to other Members.
Mr. Speaker, you are the embodiment of the spirit of parliamentary reform as exemplified by the McGrath Report, because you are the first Speaker of the House of Commons who was elected by Members of this House in a secret ballot, so as to be the servant of this House and its Members, but not to serve the Government or the governing Party of the day. You have the mandate to protect the spirit of parliamentary reform.
I would like to point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who is also the Hon. Member for Charlevoix, after the McGrath Report was released said that one of the accomplishments he and his Government would be remembered for, and maybe the only accomplishment, would be parliamentary reform. So he certainly believed in this parliamentary reform and was very supportive of the recommendations of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons presided over by the
April 25, 1989

Hon. James McGrath. I would like to quote this report, chapter 2. It is the confidence convention which is re-examined, particularly page 9 that deals with attitudi-nal change:
Free votes have customarily been allowed on such matters of conscience as capital punishment, but our proposal extends and goes beyond that principle. Implementing this practice would call for a change in attitude on the part of governments.
It would also call for a change of attitude on the part of opposition Parties, which would cease to be able to extract the maximum political advantage from defeat of government measures. They also would need to reciprocate by relaxing discipline of their own supporters.
But if neither government nor opposition Parties could be persuaded to change their attitudes, it would still be open to Private Members to take the initiative by changing theirs. Once elected, Members of Parliament are legally and constitutionally entitled to act independently.
On line 24 the report continues:
Rigid discipline is hardly compatible with the philosophy of a democratic political party, and reasonable latitude consistent with loyalty to the Party should be permitted the individual members of any Party.
I would like to quote again from page 10 on the positive effect of dissent:
The expression of dissent can have positive effects for both the institution of Parliament and its Members. It may have a direct and sometimes observable impact on public policy. As a result of defeated measures, the threat of defeat, or simple dissent not entailing defeat, governments might modify or withdraw certain measures. This opens the way for the House to become more vital and significant in influencing policy than it has been for a long time and a more accurate reflection of Canadian opinion. Private Members should take the lead in impressing this on the leadership of their respective Parties.
One Member taking an independent stand might end up paying a heavy political price, but a sizeable body of Members following the same line could not be ignored. Private Members could exert their own pressures, even cross-Party pressures, but this kind of initiative would require new procedures and new attitudes-Ideally, we would like to see a change of attitude on all sides.
Those quotes, Mr. Speaker, are made in the spirit of putting you in a position to understand why I raise this serious question on a point of privilege.
In that spirit of parliamentary reform, I have served my constituents in the Thirty-third Parliament. As ViceChairman of the Official Languages Committee I voted in the House against Bill C-72, because I felt that it discriminated against unilingual Canadians, and I

As a member of the Standing Committee of Justice and the Solicitor General, I voted on many occasions with the opposition Parties, when I felt that it was in the interest of improving a given Bill. When the Meech Lake Accord came before the House, I voted for the amendments and recorded my final vote as an abstention.
On Bill C-71, the War Criminals Act, I did not give unanimous consent because I wanted this Bill to go to committee and be studied clause by clause instead of being rushed through Parliament without being debated properly.
During the election campaign of November, 1988, I made a commitment to my constituents that I would continue to represent them in the spirit of parliamentary reform. I made it clear to the electorate of Calgary Northeast in my literature and at the door that I will oppose any tax reform that will be done on the backs of small business and the consumer.

This is a role which arose a long time ago on the basis of a perceived need in parliamentarians who have long passed on. It has continued over the ages and continues around the world because there is a role and there is a place.
I think that the role and the place begins on behalf of the institution of Parliament. It is the institution of Parliament which protects us all in a society and protects our democratic traditions and tries to make sure that a Parliament functions as well as it can at any particular time in any particular place on behalf of the citizens of a country.

Once a year there is an occasion, just after Labour Day, for the Striking Committee to meet to change committee memberships. In between the membership belongs to the Member who was appointed by this House to the committee. This House concurred unanimously in our recent report which set up the membership that now prevails in our standing committees.
The potential for public scrutiny of those assignments is of that order. That is what parliamentary reform said it should be. It said that it should be a striking committee. It said that the report should be public and in the hands of all Members of this Chamber. The Members, all of us, had to concur in that report to set up these committees. There was not a voice raised in dissent, including the voice of the Hon. Member for Calgary Northeast.
What are those new responsibilities? Because the membership resides in the Members, we have an obligation in our Standing Orders for the Member to put forward to the Clerk a list of personal substitutes. Failure to put forward that list automatically ends the membership on the committee. That is because the seat belongs to the Member and the Member has to put forward substitutes.
