I received notification from the Member for Winnipeg-Transcona (Mr. Blaikie), when I came into the House today at approximately 2.10 p.m. that: "I will be raising a point of privilege concerning answers you gave me on Chernobyl". He signed the note.
I can only make one or two points. Shortly after the Chernobyl incident took place I was obligated to go to Geneva to the World Health Conference. I told my officials that I intended to make everything public that we had in respect of the Chernobyl incident.
The reason I raised the Geneva situation is that even from Geneva, where I was for three nights, I believe, I reported to the national press here in Ottawa on any details that I was picking up in Geneva. That was obviously an issue at the World Health Organization in Geneva at the time, events just having happened shortly prior to the convening of the annual meeting of the WHO. As well, I was getting information from Canada with respect to my Department.
The Hon. Member is correct. When I returned, he and I had a number of exchanges, both inside the House and outside the House, about information relating to the effect of Chernobyl on Canada, principally Canada's North and its effect on the food chain in the North relating to the absorption of radioactive materials through lichen, eventually to the caribou and then humans.
Additionally, there was a very close monitoring by the radiation unit of the Department of National Health and Welfare of any other radiation that might be occurring in other parts of Canada. There were geographic divisions of Canada relating to the type of fallout that might be possible, and we were monitoring that on a constant basis. I was receiving a 24-hour report, and if anything untoward was happening, I would receive a report more frequently than that.
April 25, 1989

I said repeatedly to my officials at the Department of National Health and Welfare that the way I was going to handle the Chernobyl incident was to make available to the public, either through the House or through press conferences, every scintilla of information that came to hand in the belief that if information was given to Canadians, they could then make informed decisions. The Government would not use any governmental privilege to hold back any material.
All I can say as a Member of the House is that those were my instructions. To my recollection, everything that came to hand I made public. If there were other studies that have become public or have been drawn to the Hon. Member's notice, I was not aware of them, and that is where I stand as a Member of this House.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to draw the attention of Hon. Members to one of the most ambitious projects of the Government of Canada, the national policy on entrepreneurship. It is ambitious because it required a series of consultations that were almost unprecedented in this country.
We are not talking about a policy designed to camouflage reality and with practically no long-term benefits. It is not an opportunity for politicians to enhance their public image and dazzle the public with a shower of millions of dollars in grants.
There is quite a difference, Madam Speaker, between the usual financial assistance given by the Government to sectors where such assistance can be justified and adopting a genuine policy with guidelines that may influence the course of events for years to come.
In this particular case, I defy anyone to say that this is an exercise in deceit. The national entrepreneurship policy is the result of intense consultation for more than two years with every possible party with a concern in this area, all of whom were able to make their priorities known to federal officials.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
We systematically reviewed all our small business assistance programs to determine their relevance and to make any changes suggested by those on the receiving end. The decision to carry out this review was not made on the spur of the moment. We felt that the sweeping changes taking place in our economic and social climate made it incumbent upon us to get involved. There is so much going on in this world of ours that we cannot afford to leave Canada's small business people to their own devices, and we must not forget, Madam Speaker, that the Government appreciates the decisive role played by small businesses across this country. Small businesses are the principal generators of employment, and they are started by people with a great sense of innovation and drive, the real go-getters.
Experience has shown time and time again that small businesses have the peculiar ability to adapt quickly to change. The reason is that in small businesses, the decision-making process is often simplified. Small businesses learned years ago to adjust to changing circumstances and to get their share of the pie through sheer tenacity. Small businesses may be well managed and well motivated, however, but that does not make them any less vulnerable when confronted with the tremendous technological upheaval that has taken place during the last decade and is expected to accelerate as we near the year 2000.
Madam Speaker, we not only have a duty to preserve existing small businesses, we must prepare for the next generation, since the Canadian economy is largely dependent on this type of enterprise.
Entrepreneurship is a dynamic mechanism that makes it possible for companies to renew themselves. It is not the prerogative of a small group. In fact, it should be possible for every business.
Aware of changing circumstances that demanded new solutions, the Government decided to make entrepreneurship one of the linch-pins of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology.
I wish to recall this policy statement here, because from it flow all the measures taken by us and by our partners to enable small businesses to grow and to create a vast pool of entrepreneurs.
The policy of the federal Government thus involves mobilizing entrepreneurship for the purposes of the economic, social and cultural development of all regions of the country, with the participation of the private sector, provincial and territorial governments and the academic community.
This definition well summarizes the Government's deep and irreversible commitment to those who contribute day after day to building a strong Canadian economy.
The Government takes seriously the hopes, concerns and plans of Canada's entrepreneurs and the purpose of the new policy we have adopted is therefore to promote and encourage entrepreneurship while eliminating obstacles to the creation of businesses.
Among other things, this means that we wish to sensitize all kinds of potential entrepreneurs and not only those who were called "family heads" in the past. The target group of potential entrepreneurs has grown considerably in recent years.
I do not have to stress, Madam Speaker, the most spectacular rise of women in the business world. Examples of successful women have become so numerous and commonplace that very few people now pay much attention to it, except perhaps in some professions traditionally considered male bastions.
We have other target groups that previous Governments did not always deal with properly. For example, I want to talk about the young people who aspire very early to economic independence, native people, seniors, the elderly and new Canadians.
If our social climate provides enough encouragement to entrepreneurship, we will see a flowering of "entrepreneurial culture".
We have agreed to adopt many initiatives. I shall mention only a few, Madam Speaker.
First, the creation of a national entrepreneurship development institute is one of our top priorities. This institute will be a focal point for research, information and creative ideas on entrepreneurship. All those interested will have easy access to it, whether they are in business or teaching.
The national institute that we will establish is not meant to take the place of the educational programs offered throughout the country. Its role will rather be complementary; it will expand on and modernize the very concept of entrepreneurship and make it more attractive.
April 25, 1989

Unlike the United States, very few Canadian educational institutions emphasize the entrepreneurial spirit. As a result, students attach little importance to self-employment and business creation in choosing their career.
It is not surprising that in such a context, Madam Speaker, many professions are subject to strict quotas and it is increasingly difficult for students to have a university education in many so-called classical disciplines.
We must therefore keep a critical eye on all obstacles to entrepreneurship and consider fiscal measures to stimulate the entrepreneurial spirit. Among the obstacles most often mentioned is the flood of federal paperwork that has caused many nightmares for small corporations that have neither the time nor the resources to handle it. Too much paperwork is also damaging to the perception of the Government too many people still have, namely that governments hurt more often than help those who call upon them.
In this regard, the federal Government adopted a plan of action in May 1987 to reduce paperwork, resulting in the creation of an advisory committee on the subject. Through that committee, small businesses can propose ways to gradually reduce forms, statistical research and other forms of red tape.
Parliament will now receive an annual report on the status of small business in Canada, which will give all those concerned the information they need to take stock and plan for their future.
The Government also favors promoting regional development by emphasizing regional decision making so that small businesses will have more say in the matter and be able to influence the development of programs affecting them.
We also have the firm intention of promoting entrepreneurship in the public opinion, which is one way to reach non-traditional groups of entrepreneurs I talked about earlier.
Madam Speaker, with advertising campaigns and the establishment of prestigious forums to spread our message, we will show Canadians the benefits of owning a business.
Industry, Science and Technology
Certainly, the Department of Industry, Science and Technology will continue to give its Canada Awards for Business Excellence, which bring to the general public's attention the exceptional accomplishments of big and small entrepreneurs. We have noticed that these awards are increasingly coveted, and the growing number of competing companies confirms their validity.
With respect to another issue, I would be remiss if I did not stress that a new national entrepreneurship policy would never have seen the light of day had it not been for the favourable federal-provincial climate of co-operation. As it happens, the various levels of government meet regularly and, generally speaking, their exchanges take place harmoniously, a far cry from the pre-1984 power struggles. There can be no doubt that the stabilization of relations with our partners is the major factor behind the implementation-in relatively short time-of a multi-faceted entrepreneurship policy.
Madam Speaker, I would remind you that thanks to a program developed with the co-operation of Supply and Services Canada, small businesses can more easily bid on public contracts. In addition, the program designed to promote sub-contracting makes allowance for the establishment of new positions for small business ombudsmen within the Supply and Services Canada purchasing system.
In my estimation this goes to show that the Government of Canada did not limit the scope of its entrepreneurship policy to the department directly involved. On the contrary, we step in whenever we can foster the spirit of entrepreneurship, even at the risk of playing havoc with certain programs sponsored by other departments.
And so it will be at every stage of implementation of the entrepreneuship policy. The active participation of all kinds of agencies will become ever more necessary, and they will co-operate even more closely regardless of the progress which may or may not have been accomplished thus far. The innovation spirit of our policy will enable us to extend throughout the country the scope of successful endeavours adapted to other levels.
Such is the case, among others, of the Canada investment opportunity network which proved to be quite effective in Ontario and which is being extended to the rest of the country.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Operated with the participation of various chambers of commerce, it brings together people who have challenging ideas and others who are looking for promising investment opportunities. Combining new ideas and capital investment will give renewed vigour to the creation of new businesses, and that can only benefit all Canadians.
I must simply say a few words about the small business and entrepreneurship office whose mission is to support the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Hockin) in Cabinet. The office is responsible for formulating and evaluating policies that are relevant to small business and to national programs for this sector.
Here we have an agency with very concrete terms of reference, since it has the authority to order studies, to carry out analyses and to make recommendations for scrutiny by the Minister or Cabinet. The entrepreneurship and small business office embodies and consolidates the Government's principal instruments for supporting small businesses.
Madam Speaker, some Hon. Members may still wonder why we are putting so much energy into defending and promoting small businesses. My answer is that 98.8 per cent of Canadian businesses are small businesses. If we don't take care of them, we are headed for an economic impasse.
The term small business designates companies that employ fewer than 100 employees in the manufacturing sector and fewer than 50 in the services sector. The total number of small businesses across the country is 812,000, while the total number of companies registered in Canada is 822,000.
They are found in all industrial sectors, and in fact they are the majority. In the primary industries, small businesses represent 99.9 per cent of all companies: transportation, communications, mining and manufacturing, construction, finance, and so forth, and it is accurate to say that small businesses still represent over 98 per cent of the total number of companies.
In the past we have often said, with the figures to prove it, that small businesses were the best job creators.
However, small business' contribution to research and development is often overlooked. Our studies in this respect prove there is no doubt about that. The percentage of spending on research and development is higher among businesses with fewer than 50 employees. In fact,
we found that the smaller the enterprise, the greater the relative share spent on research and development.
We concluded that because of their energy and drive, small businesses were far better able than we expected to adapt to technological change.
This is good news for free trade, whose initial consequence will be to stimulate the growth of small businesses eager to enter the North American market. This means that our exportable small businesses will have to follow the technological change that will prevail in the United States, especially in the so-called vulnerable sectors.
The Government is not overly concerned by that indirect effect of free trade, because our small businesses have shown long ago that they can adjust faster than big companies to market fluctuations and technological changes.
Certainly, Madam Speaker, our small businesses will have to change, by specializing and offering unique services, for example. They must also improve productivity and aim for excellence at all times.
As we said before, the Free Trade Agreement is not a seven-headed ogre waiting to devour the weakest in the coming months. Custom duties are being eliminated over a ten-year period and protective mechanisms have been put in place so that less competitive sectors will have time to adjust to the new trade environment.
In addition, the Department of Industry, Science and Technology will propose new programs to give small business better access to new technologies. They will therefore have time to improve their productivity and competitiveness as free trade is being gradually implemented.
Madam Speaker, Canadians have been informed, I am sure, of the main recommandations made by the Adjustment Committee in what the media dubbed the "de Grandpre Report".
It is not my responsibility to elaborate on its detailed contents but I want to bring to your attention the excellent grade the commissioners gave the Canadian Government for its series of measures already in place to make adjustment easier.
In fact, there are more than 400 programs to help employers and employees flexibly join a labour market where technological change is an everyday reality. Many of these training and adjustment programs are sponsored by Employment and Immigration Canada. Madam Speaker, it is not an exaggeration to say that the Government correctly foresaw the major world trends that would affect our country's labour force.
April 25, 1989

Since 1984, "adjustment" is part of the vocabulary of our elected officials and has guided their most important policies. In large part, this explains why the de Grandpre Report did not recommend a thorough overhaul of our programs.
One minute more. Madam Speaker, and I am through. The Government foresaw the arrival of a one-way technological wave. We had to follow along because the survival of the Canadian economy depended on it. Gradually, we made some changes like reforming the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to be in step with the new world economic realities.
Today, Madam Speaker, we have resources and policies that let us look ahead with optimism. Everything is already in place. We just hope that all Canadians, men and women, will follow along and support us in reaching our economic destiny which is so promising.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for his speech. He is certainly aware of what is happening in this field. He is certainly very interested in this subject.
I have in my hand a report published by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which contains several recommendations that a task force made for industries and to inform politicians on the federal level.

I will just quote a couple of paragraphs from this report. First, it talks about bureaucratic objectives rather than market impulses which have prevailed in Canadian science and technology policy. Further it reads:
Without a private sector agenda and forum for discussion, the government programs that have emerged do not necessarily stimulate entrepreneurial initiative. In most cases they provide funds for technology development and innovation -
It goes on to the point where the task force suggests the following:
It is the opinion of the task force that despite the proliferation of activities during the past year in the area of technology policy, business has lost ground in defining the agenda.
Industry, Science and Technology
The Government has done quite a bit over past few years in setting up the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney); in setting up InovAction-the Canadian Strategy for Science and Technology; in setting up the federal-provincial science and technology subagreements; in setting up the industry led advisory boards which were established by the National Research Council and so on; and in setting up the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology.
Those are all very commendable initiatives. Unfortunately, in the area of research and development, when we compare Canada with the rest of the industrialized world, we are falling way behind with the amount of financial support from the private sector and the number of scientists per million that we have.
While industry over and over again, both in the private and in the public sector, is suggesting that rather than throwing money at the problem the role of the Government should be to provide tax incentives and to act as a facilitator to the industry. Therefore, it is entrusted in seeing more focus on the area of development rather than on pure science and research. Pure science does not lead to anything unless it is put into application.
Does the Hon. Member see the Government moving in the right direction in putting more funds into setting up an agency, or does he see it working better with the private sector, and also the other partners in the provinces?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Harb) just said, I think my speech more or less reflects the 28 years I spent in the private sector and in manufacturing. When we consider an issue as general as basic research or technology, we must consider what part of the country we are talking about. We know for instance that Ontario, the province where the Hon. Member's riding is located, receives the lion's share of federal funding for research and development. Our counterparts in Quebec have complained that the federal Government does not invest enough money in research and development, and I must say. Madam Speaker, that I am enclined to believe what the Government of Quebec has told us in this respect. These are things that might be changed in the weeks to come.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
I also wanted to say that I am from a riding Kamouras-ka-Riviere-du-Loup that qualifies as a remote area. We have no businesses with 2,000, 3,000 or 4,000 employees in Eastern Quebec. We have small businesses. As a person who has been exposed to and has promoted this kind of business in the past, I can say that research and development was done by the businesses themselves.
I have nothing against what they teach in universities. In the speeches I heard this morning, there was great emphasis on putting a lot of money into the universities for research and development. I agree, but money should also go to industry.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, I would like to give you an example. In 1984, when I was the elected representative for Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup, I decided we should do something about the peat lands. As you know, the area is very rich in peat. Before, people used to bag peat moss and export it to the United States for use in horticulture. However, since 1984, we now have a peat research centre that belongs to Tourbiere Premier and is going to expand within the next few months. We also have a research centre that was developed at the Riviere-du-Loup Cegep, also for peat. Since 1984, Riviere-du-Loup no longer has any doubts about the peat market, because through the research and development done with industry and with the help of the public sector and the Cegep we have no universities in our area we managed to develop a market that has now become quite substantial.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It gives me a great deal of pleasure to address the House this afternoon on Bill C-3. In the Government's repeal of the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion Act, the federal Government's creation of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology may appear to be constructive enough. Its aims, some of which include the development, implementation and promotion of national policies to foster international competitiveness of industry, enhancement of industrial, scientific and technological development and so on, as outlined in Part I of Bill C-3, might also appear to be attractive.
The object is obviously an attempt to elevate science to full department status. The question remains as to whether the Government's restructuring is merely cosmetic. Staff morale continues to be low, and at the committee level there is not much hope for any positive change in the Government's commitment to science and technology.
The Government's track record in the area of science and technology, and research and development has been for the past four years, to say the least, dismal.
Let us look at the Government's actual performance in this area. Research and development is the essential impetus for technological development, the foundation of today's high technology companies. As the high tech capital of Canada, therefore research and development is particularly important to my Nepean riding which represents more than 100 high tech companies. Nepean is the home of Canada's largest research and development organization, Bell Northern Research.
This company has pioneered fully digital telecommunications technology, and employs 4,200 people locally. Northern Telecom, also in Nepean, of which BNR is a subsidiary, is Canada's largest telecommunication equipment supplier, specializing in voice and data communications, and employs 1,400 people locally. CDC, Computing Devices of Canada, employs 1,300 people in Nepean. They produce advanced electronic systems for military and commercial use world-wide. Gandalf, which specializes in information networking systems such as modems, multiplexes, data switches and large network processes, employs 650 people in Nepean. These are only four of over 100 companies working in the technological field, our largest employers that were developed in full co-operation and assistance from government, not in spite of them.
Beyond Nepean's boundaries in our sister cities are high tech companies of international status, such as the Mitel Corporation, Digital, Cognos, Lumonics and Sys-temhouse, just to name a few. Practically all of these companies started out in someone's garage or basement. Most were on the receiving end of research and development grants from the then Liberal federal Government. Young companies today need the same infusion of money through research and development, or start-up grants, as their counterparts did, if they are to survive in an international market. It is an international competitiveness, as the Canadian market is not sufficient to sustain the high tech industry.
April 25, 1989

Ottawa Carleton Regional Government, along with Carleton University, Ottawa University, Algonquin College and leaders in the high tech community have created an organization called the Ottawa Carleton Research Institute. The institute monitors what is happening in the high tech field. The industry works with the universities to ensure that our students are being trained in the latest technology.
On December 1, 1988, the Province of Ontario formed TRIO, the Telecommunications Research Institute of Ontario. Its new president comes from Bell Northern Research. Its role is to understand university-driven technology. Coupling the institute with industry will give businesses the opportunity to better position themselves vis-a-vis technology. However, the Government has proceeded to cut back in different areas in Environment Canada at a time when Canadians are more concerned with the environment than ever before in history. The Government has cut back on energy research, completely wiping out the energy department at the National Research Council when it should be cutting back on Canada's reliance on fossil fuels and developing environmentally cleaner energy sources.
A program also being worked on by Energy, Mines and Resources when major cut-backs happened at EMR caused the cancellation of this research. With the lessons of the softwood lumber a recent and bitter memory, and the needs of the forest industry and what the forest industry does for Canada as outlined in "Wood Leader'', it is important that Canada increase the yields from its forests by increasing the effort and money put into research and development.
The Government has cut back at Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. when it should be looking at the exciting opportunities presented by the recent developments in fusion technology.
The Government has cut back in every area of basic research. Those areas particularly hard hit by cuts to government point to short-term gain for long-term pain.
In addition, the Government has allowed important issues to be governed by politics rather than what is best for the industry concerned, and I might cite a few examples. The CF-18 contract was taken away from Manitoba. The space agency was moved from the Na-
Industry, Science and Technology
tional Capital Region in spite of repeated briefs from the industry that it was in the nation's best interest to locate in the nation's capital. Canada now has the exclusive role of being the only country in the world where the administering body to the space industry is located outside its capital.
The fact is that research and development has suffered badly under the present Government.
Total expenditure on research and development as a percentage of the Gross Domestic Product has decreased from an all-time high of almost 1.4 per cent during the Liberal administration four years ago to a low of 1.35 per cent during the past four years. This Government must be committed to increasing R and D expenditures to at least 2.5 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product in line with that of other major industrial nations in the world.
Canada presently ranks last among the G-7 nations. As well, research and development expenditures were roughly half those of other nations in the world.
The Government has consistently spoken the praises of R and D on the one hand while decimating Canada's effort on the other, from the well publicized cuts to the National Research Council of over $100 million to the reduction of the R and D tax credit to 75 per cent.
In my riding Northern Telecom Electronics cut 60 jobs at its Nepean plant, and several other firms have also laid off many employees.
High interest rates threaten the viability of other high-tech companies, and in terms of government investment Nepean has lost millions of dollars of research and development related activity over the past four years.
The $90 million animal virus laboratory slated for Nepean was initially cancelled and is now moved elsewhere. Government cuts to research and development tax incentives have cost companies like BNR and Gan-dalf millions.
In terms of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, another warning sign to note is the fact that the 34-member National Advisory Committee on Science and Technology, chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and touted as a signal of his commitment, has not met since last summer.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
The Liberal position in the area of science and technology and research and development is clear. We condemn the Government for breaking its promise to double Canada's R and D effort to 2.5 per cent of the GNP and for the measures announced since September, 1984, which are undermining R and D, long-term economic growth, and the competitiveness of Canadian business in world markets.
We condemn the Conservative approach to R and D funding in Canada as inefficient and damaging to Canadian industries, particularly to small business, which brings me back to my original point.
Is the federal Government's action in its creation of this new Department merely cosmetic? Is the Government addressing the real issue? How does the Government answer to the research and development cut-backs it has implemented? How does the Government plan to deal effectively with the issues of decentralization and regional development?
The federal Government's credibility, in its consistency on science and technology research and development policy, is at stake. In the creation of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, in conjunction with its actual track record in this area, the Government has given and taken with the same hand.
The cut-backs at the National Research Council should be rescinded and the commitment to provide funding for basic research should be reaffirmed, and the base budget of granting councils must be increased above inflation, along with university research. The Government must look for imaginative ways of increasing the technology transfer to industry and assisting industry in the critical early stages of the start of a high-tech company.

However, eastern Ontario was omitted completely from any consideration in terms of being mentioned as an area that needed further economic development. I want to bring that to the attention of my colleague and ask if she has noted that, as I did, particularly in light of comments made by a certain Member from the Mississauga area shortly after the last election to the effect that eastern Ontario was not going to be rewarded for having chosen to elect 12 out of 14 Members who are of a political persuasion different from that of the present Government.
I ask my colleague if she would agree with me that eastern Ontario certainly deserves all the consideration that it traditionally received from all Governments, be they Liberal or Conservative, and if she agrees with me as well that rural eastern Ontario is still disadvantaged economically and requires special attention from this new Ministry which we are talking of establishing so that we can attract industry into eastern Ontario and get our fair share of the economic pie.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to speak on Bill C-3, an Act to establish the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, to repeal the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts.
In the debate today Members on this side of the House, and I hope Members opposite, will have an opportunity to bring out some of the concerns we have with respect to economic development in Canada, which is the subject matter of the motion we are debating this afternoon. To give a brief description of this legislation, it is to establish in law-to create-the Department of Industry, Science and Technology which will replace the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, which has had most of its functions replaced by the Atlantic Opportunities Agency and the Western Diversification Office. As the previous speaker said, these two entities will be meshed together in an attempt to have industrial policy in science and technology within the same Department.
Industry, Science and Technology
It is creditable that the Government should undertake such a measure. As the debate goes on, it will be carried by our critics who are stick-handling this particular discussion from our side of the House. I refer to the Hon. Member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair (Mr. McCurdy) and the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) who will be discussing the Bill further as it proceeds through the House.
We are debating today a motion moved by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor. I would like to read it since it points out the importance that Members on this side of the House place on the debate we have leading up to the Budget on Thursday in terms of our economic development. The motion states:
"this House declines to give second reading to Bill C-3 because it fails to clearly define federal Government responsibility for regional development and specifically fails to reflect the requirement under s. 36(l)(b) of the Constitution Act, 1982 that Parliament is committed to "furthering economic development to reduce disparity in opportunities"."
The concern now is with respect to what we will see in the Budget on Thursday night. In my discussion I would like to focus on what my research has turned up in terms of the vehicles for that economic development which I suggest will be threatened on Thursday night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) as well as what may be suggested in the future.
I want to focus on what is a critical development tool in my Province of British Columbia. I think the same applies to other provinces as well. I refer to the forestry agreements which come under the umbrella of economic agreements which the Government currently has up for review. It is revealing that at this point in time there are economic agreements in limbo with some six provinces. In fact, official negotiations have not even started in those agreements. Particularly revealing is the importance that this has to all Members in those areas, be it with respect to tourism, mining or forestiy. It is shocking to see that we have reached such a stage in economic development in Canada.
In British Columbia prior to the election we talked about the silent 19 Tories who had nothing to say about B.C. Their number has been reduced. They are now invisible. They are now the invisible 12. We will have to send out a search and rescue team quickly to find those Tories from B.C. They are not representing the interests of their constituents in this House, especially when the Minister of Finance will start to dismantle economic agreements and forestry agreements on Thursday night.

April 25, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
These economic agreements are vehicles by which different levels of Government can participate in economic development in a particular area. In British Columbia there is a forestry resource development agreement. We have a science and technology subagreement. We also have an agriculture subagreement, as well as agreements in mining and other areas. There has been a great deal of debate about what the Government will do with economic development in the Budget. There has been written notice given to the House that something is afoot in terms of how these agreements will be rewritten. I refer to a letter sent to me on April 18 by the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Oberle) who stated: "A full year remains in the present agreement and formal negotiations for new agreements cannot be undertaken until such time as a new economic regional development agreement policy framework has been approved by Cabinet". What is that new economic regional development agreement policy framework that is being discussed?
The Budget on Thursday will be more than a Budget of numbers. It will create a furore in the country, a furore such as Members opposite claimed was created by the National Energy Program which was introduced by the Liberals when they were in office. It is extremely important that all Members pay careful attention to the debate that follows the Budget.
We also know from comments made by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Andre) that the Government will try to change the agreements because it is not getting the credit that it wishes. I have a clipping in my hand from The Ottawa Citizen in which the Minister is quoted as having said: "Candidly, some of our members are ticked off".
Do you know what the debate comes down to. Madam Speaker? It comes down to who gets the biggest four-byeight on a project site. It is the Government's own fault if it cannot turn its incredible and massive public relations operation to obtaining a nicely painted four-byeight on a site for which it feels it should get credit. It is ludicrous to think that for some PR we will see a complete rewriting of economic development agreements. That is the level to which the debate has sunk when we talk about economic agreements in the country.
I would like to comment briefly on one particular subagreement which is critical to a great many smaller communities, such as the ones in my riding. I refer to tourism. There is a sense in my province that when it comes to assistance from the federal or provincial Government for tourist development projects or destination points, that if one is not a Whistler or a site like it then it is difficult to get the ear of the Government. If one has a development like Whistler and one needs $6 million, the Government's response is: "The cheque will be ready on Friday. Is that too late?" As most Hon. Members know there is a host of smaller tourist facilities throughout my province, as well as throughout many other areas of the country, which need some help with landscaping, sewer or electrical access and that type of thing.
If there is not a complete emasculation of the economic development agreements this Thursday night, then those types of discussions can take place, at least in British Columbia where we have an economic agreement in place, unless something happens to it. It is regrettable that the economic agreements which are currently in place are in limbo in six provinces. There are six provinces in the country which have economic agreements between the Government and their respective provincial governments that have lapsed. No official negotiations have taken place with respect to them. It is incredible that such a thing would happen and we all wonder what is going to happen after Thursday night. The importance of tourism to the provinces is to ensure that the money gets out of, in our case in British Columbia, the lower mainland, that the interior, Kamloops, the Shuswap area and North Peace, has the opportunity to access some of those funds.
I know the Member from Okanagan-Shuswap (Mr. MacWilliam), the tourism critic for our Party, raised this matter last week in the House in the debate on this motion. He put very clearly how important those opportunities are for a lot of the small tourist operators, many of them run by volunteer organizations that struggle from grant to grant, from employment program to employment program, and put in many hours of volunteer work to ensure that their particular sites are well taken care of and ready for the tourists that come and visit their area.
April 25, 1989

The economic agreements, I suggest to you, are the nature and reason for our motion. To express our concerns about what has happened to date with those economic agreements is all the more pointed out by a letter of April 12 from the Canadian Forestry Association to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) expressing concern about the renewal of those forestry agreements. The Forestry Association is making that their number one priority, because of the concern in our provinces regarding forest regeneration, the silvicultural work that has to be done in each of these areas.
On this side of the House we think that on Thursday night the Budget is going to be about more than just numbers. The correspondence that I have received from the Minister indicates there is going to be a wholesale change in the way the economic agreements currently exist between the federal Government and the provinces. It is a wholesale change that we will want to watch closely to ensure that in western Canada, at least, the right that we have in terms of the re-investment of tax dollars into our region is taken care of. We want to make sure that is done effectively.
Earlier in this session I put a question to the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Oberle) that he would give this House his assurance that it would be his Department and his Department alone that would administer the federal-provincial forestry agreements. We did not get that commitment.
I am concerned that what is going to come out of the Budget on Thursday night is going to be a funnelling, if you like, of the complete administrative control to the various agencies like the Western Diversification Fund and the Atlantic Opportunities Agency. Those are the agencies that are going to become the new channels for federal power in this country. I have some concerns about that.
In our province we have a Premier in Victoria who has created states throughout our province. Granted, in one or two places it is working. In others, it has created a whole new level of government that the various agencies have to go through. What we are seeing there and what we are going to see here is the "Zamming" of Canada from this Government on Thursday night.
Adjournment Debate
I know the debate will continue, after this motion has been disposed of, into the discussion around science and technology and the concerns that we have on this side of the House about the research that is needed in that field. But I would like to suggest to the Government before closing that it has a mandate to follow through on another election promise they made, a promise they made two elections ago. That was about the introduction of legislation to establish a Department of Forests and to create a National Forests Act. We know that the Minister of State has said that it is not a high priority of the Government. That is from the January 31 issue of The Prince George Citizen. That is regrettable, but I checked the status of Bills and motions. We have gone as far as Bill C-10. Let us see if tomorrow we can bring forward Bill C-ll, legislation to enact the National Forests Act and the Ministry of Forests so we know we can start debating that legislation as well.
In closing, I want to say that I look forward to some of the future debate on this legislation. I know the Member from Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) is aware of the work that is being done in our community for a northern university and the role that science and technology can play, and some of the representations I have made to him about the need for a forest research centre in Prince George. I think we will hear more about that in the future as we discuss science and technology as it relates to the forest industry in this country.
Most of all, I urge all Members of this House and the Canadian public to watch and listen to the Budget closely on Thursday night because I suspect that we will have a full plate to deal with. I trust this Government will listen to the concerns that we raise and that they will hear Canadians and their concerns about economic development in this country. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. Gardiner) for his remarks on Bill C-3. My comments arise from a meeting I attended in Nelson, British Columbia, last week. It was a week-long convention attended by well over 200 people in the mining industry from the Chamber of Mines in eastern British Columbia. It was the largest convention of its kind since 1933 in the southeastern part of that province. They expressed very strong concerns relating directly to this Bill. My first comment concerns the mineral development agreement. The Canada-British Columbia Mineral Development Agreement at $10 million is the smallest of the eight subagreements made under the $580 million Economic Regional Development Agreements in British Columbia.
The B.C. Mineral Development Agreement, from a Canadian perspective, is very small. The agreement is larger than those of only two provinces, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island, when the mining industry in British Columbia is one of the key employers and producers of wealth in the region.
Furthermore, the geoscience data-base in British Columbia is inferior to that of several other provinces.
Industry, Science and Technology
For instance, 90 per cent of the province remains to be mapped at a scale which is required for basic exploration in the province. Yet, this is one of the smallest agreements in Canada.
The Chamber of Mines in eastern British Columbia had several concerns, particularly with regard to Bill C-3. According to Bill C-3, the Government is eliminating the current regime for regional economic expansion. It is likely that the Budget on April 27 will result in a further removal of this whole area of regional subagreements under the Western Economic Diversification Fund, as far as western Canada is concerned.
I want to refer briefly to the British Columbia-Yukon Chambers of Mines letter written to me on March 28. It states:
We believe the Western Diversification Fund's policies and objectives are not compatible with the current structure of Mineral Development Agreements inasmuch as the Western Diversification Fund's mandate is to diversify through industry with industry delivering the product.
In a letter dated February 28, addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp), the Chamber of Mines of Eastern British Columbia said:
We have a concern that your government may confuse MDA funding with funds allocated by the Western Diversification Office. Sir, the policy and objectives of the two programs are totally incompatible: the fundamental objective of MDA is to deliver basic geoscientific data to a variety of users including government (as well as to industry to foster the discovery and development of new mines).
Does the Hon. Member share these concerns of the miners and the mining industry in British Columbia? How does he view the presumed intent of the Government to lump this in with regional development programs under the Western Diversification Fund?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a great deal of concern about Bill C-3. I think it will reduce the emphasis on regional development in this country. I believe this Bill is another step in the Government's attempt to gloss over the whole question of regional development. I believe this legislation is an attempt to isolate regional development to Ontario and Quebec, while leaving Atlantic Canada to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, western Canada to the Western Diversification Office and northern Ontario to its own fund. The Government's attitude seems to be that the regions should take care of themselves with those funds so it may concentrate on southern Ontario and Quebec. That attitude will do a tremendous amount of damage to this country.
Canada depends on regional development to keep it as a unit. Rather than Balkanize Canada, the Government should see the country as a whole to determine what areas need the most attention.
Canadians in Atlantic Canada, western Canada, and northern Canada will not have their lives pigeonholed with these various development programs. The Government cannot shift its responsibilities to these various regional development agencies and still maintain this country as the great unit it has been since Confederation. That concept which the Government is trying to create is totally unacceptable. The Government will try to make Atlantic Canadians believe that this approach will be beneficial to them.
It could be beneficial to Atlantic Canadians if the Government really wanted to develop the concept of regional development. It could be beneficial if the Government, without political patronage, wanted to develop Atlantic Canada and do what was best for the various areas of Atlantic Canada. The same is true of western Canada and northern Canada. The Government
should treat these regions as a part of Canada. However, this is not what is being done.
I am afraid that the concept of regional development is being gradually whittled away. The thrust of this originated with the Free Trade Agreement. There is no definition of a subsidy in the Free Trade Agreement. The Government wants us to believe that regional development will not be considered a subsidy. However, that is not what the Americans are saying. They are saying that regional development is considered a subsidy. This is evidenced by the decision taken regarding Sydney Steel Corporation.
A countervail has been placed against Sydney Steel Corporation by the United States Department of Commerce, a countervail in the amount of 103.55 per cent. How was that figure reached? The Department of Commerce listed every bit of government assistance the Sydney Steel Corporation receives, either federal or provincial, and applied a certain percentage of countervail against each item. It came up with the figure of 103.55 per cent.
Sydney Steel Corporation is in an area that is undergoing economic difficulties right now. The programs Sydney Steel took advantage of were programs that were made available by the federal and provincial Governments. It is a provincial Crown corporation which did not break any laws, but if this American countervail is ratified, Sydney Steel will suffer but not as a result of Canadian law. The company took advantage of Canadian programs that were made available and it obeyed the laws of Canada. As a result of the Free Trade Agreement, it will be punished retroactively by the laws of the United States of America.
Regional development is becoming something that is determined by the United States of America. Any industry that locates in Atlantic Canada, northern Canada or western Canada and receives a subsidy from the Government or the respective province will be seen by the United States as a company that is receiving a subsidy. Because it is seen as a company that receives a subsidy, the company will be countervailed against when it exports into the United States. It will be punished by that agreement which was supposed to be of such benefit to all Canada, an agreement that was supposed to help Canadians living in the regions that were undergoing economic difficulties. Instead, we are being punished by it.
April 25, 1989

We in Atlantic Canada were told that the trade agreement would be the salvation of the economy because we would be able to ship things made in Atlantic Canada by water to the eastern United States. That would be wonderful if we could do so without punishment. It would be of tremendous benefit. I do not hesitate to say that.
Before Confederation the natural markets of Atlantic Canada were in the eastern United States and the West Indies because goods were shipped by water and water transportation is the cheapest form of transportation. If a company locates in Atlantic Canada and receives assistance from the federal Government or the province, and if in turn it is judged by the United States to have received a subsidy because of regional development assistance and is countervailed against with a 7 per cent penalty, how can we expect the company to compete?
What is the Free Trade Agreement doing for Atlantic Canada? It is a catch-22 situation. We will be worse off if the United States perceives that we have broken an agreement that was entered into between the two countries. It would not be a rule of thumb of the U.S. Congress. It would be a determination by the United States that we breached an agreement entered into with the United States.
We have entered into a trade agreement with the United States. That could be very beneficial, but if you went to a lawyer, Madam Speaker, and said that you wanted an agreement that would allow you to carry on your business in a certain way, an agreement on which you could rely, and then you went back in a month's time and the lawyer said that the agreement was ready but there were a couple of clauses that had not yet been defined, but told you to sign the agreement and he would fill in the definitions later, you would get another lawyer. If you did not, one would wonder why you did not. However, this is what Canada did. It has said it would sign the agreement without specifying that regional development is not a subsidy.
We are now subject to the American determination of a subsidy and the Americans think that regional development assistance is a subsidy. I say this because of the Sydney Steel Corporation example. The Department of Commerce of the Government of the United States, not an ad hoc body, has put a percentage figure beside every subsidy Sydney Steel receives from the federal and provincial Governments, added up those percentages and came out with the figure of 103.55 per cent for a countervail. In today's competitive market, if it were a 5
Industry, Science and Technology
per cent countervail, it would be difficult for Sydney Steel to sell its products in the United States. However, the countervail is 103.55 per cent.
Two of the items included in that list are ERDAs and General Development Agreements. Those are the backbone of the regional development program. What could be less offensive than an ERDA or a GDA? This is funding entered into through an agreement between the federal Government and the provinces. Since Nova Scotia is considered to be a province that is having more economic difficulty than Ontario, for example, the federal Government may contribute more to an agreement with it than it would to an agreement with Ontario. These agreements cover various aspects of the economy including agriculture, fisheries and forestry.
Included in that list compiled by the United States Department of Commerce is the assistance Sydney Steel Corporation receives under ERDAs and GDAs. These are considered subsidies by the Government of the United States. That is a frightening situation of very great concern.
The Government has stated that it is not going to sign any ERDA agreements until after the Budget. Why is the Government saying that? As the lesser of the two evils the Government would like us to think that because it has to get into a cost cutting mode it is going to cut out regional development assistance. However, what the Government is not saying is that it is not a question of cutting out regional development assistance in the Budget. It is a question that it has already given away the right to regional development assistance through the Free Trade Agreement with the United States.
The Budget has nothing to do with it. In the matter of regional development we are going to be restricted to infrastructure agreements with municipalities and agreements that do not relate in any way to specific industries that may, will, or, by some hope in the future, have any trade with the United States. If those industries in Canada receive any assistance they will be countervailed by the United States.
That is treachery against the areas of the country that were hoping to increase their economic performance and to reduce economic disparity instead of having that economic disparity widen. It is treacherous that the Government signed an agreement without having all of the definitions filled out and meaningful clauses put in. The Government bailed out on the "have not" areas of the country.

April 25. 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) is now saying that it will take seven years to define a subsidy. He also stated: "What two countries have been able to agree on what is a subsidy?" That is cold comfort now, after we entered into the agreement which was finalized four months ago.
The Minister tells us that it will be the full seven years and that we should not expect a definition of a subsidy because in his opinion no two countries have ever been able to agree on the definition of a subsidy.
That certainly is cold comfort for people in Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, and large parts of western Canada who hoped to be able to close the economic disparity gap. They were told by the Government that that gap was going to be closed. Instead it is widening, and the Government is fostering that at the present time. That is the problem and that is the misleading that has been going on.
What are the ramifications going to be? Those people who would have established in Atlantic Canada because they were on tide water and could ship from a port in Atlantic Canada to tide water in the United States and take advantage of one of the cheaper means of transportation, will not be able to do that now. If they receive assistance from the province or the federal Government to relocate in Atlantic Canada, they will not be able to ship into the United States without a countervail because the American Government will consider that they have received a subsidy.
In this Act the Government is belittling the whole scheme of regional development. Gradually it is erasing it from the vocabulary of Canadians. This is happening at a time when it is particularly difficult in areas such as Atlantic Canada. In Atlantic Canada, northern Canada, and western Canada people have to deal with higher interest rates. The Government is now telling us that we have to deal with those higher interest rates because we have to cool down the economy in southern Ontario.
Why is the Government now saying that the economy in southern Ontario has to be cooled down? The Government previously stated that it could not reduce the deficit more because that would cause a decline in the activity in southern Ontario and in other parts of the country. It would throw cold water on the economic revival. That is why the deficit could not be further
reduced. Yet we are now being told that the deficit has to be reduced more and that we have to cool down the economy in southern Ontario. Right across the country people will have to bear the brunt of higher interest rates.
The other side of the coin is extremely interesting. While the economy in southern Ontario has to be cooled down, the economy in Atlantic Canada certainly does not need to be cooled down. Far from it. It needs to be fostered by the Government with some action instead of platitudes and excuses.
However, we are going to have the economy in Atlantic Canada cooled down anyway because high interest rates apply across the country. Because of the Government's policy of deregulation in the airline industry we now have Air Canada and Canadian Airlines International forming subsidiary companies. In northern Ontario and in western Canada those subsidiary companies are being formed. In Atlantic Canada we have Air Nova, which is a subsidiary of Air Canada, and Air Atlantic, which is a subsidiary of Canadian Airlines International. Air Canada and Canadian Airlines are to cut down service to some of the less populated areas, not in the major centres.
However, they are also stating: "Lucky you in Atlantic Canada, because you are going to get more flights". We are to get a Dash-8 service sponsored by Air Nova or Air Atlantic. Jump up and down because this is a great day is what they would have us believe.
There will be more flights, but there will be less capacity for cargo. The big problem is that Air Canada employees in those areas where service is being phased out will all have to take severance pay, early retirement, or move to some other location. The people who will work for Air Nova and Air Atlantic will be replacing those employees who worked for Air Canada and Canadian Airlines. They will only be paid 50 per cent to 60 per cent of what Canadian Airlines and Air Canada employees were paid. They are only to receive 50 per cent to 60 per cent for doing the same work that was done by employees of Air Canada and Canadian Airlines. They will be doing the same work done by those people employed in Halifax, Montreal, and Toronto. The same work is being done in the major centres, but those people in the major centres are paid considerably more.
April 25, 1989

That is the Government's idea of regional development. This Bill is only another step further along the road to widening the disparity gap between the major centres and those areas undergoing economic difficulties at the present time. It is a big step backward and another step backward fostered by the Government.

Industry, Science and Technology

At the same time it is a Government in charge of the country's economy.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-CHANGE TO SYSTEM-EFFECT ON RURAL AREAS-EFFECT OF CHANGES ON NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to express my dissatisfaction with an answer given by the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) to a question that I raised in the House of Commons on April 17.
The Government of Canada, on April 11, established what it called its labour force development strategy. That is a euphemism for cutting back on UIC. This plan is in conflict with solemn promises made by the Government of Canada during the election campaign. I am sure, Madam Speaker, you being the non-partisan person that you are would want to be apprised of what the Minister responsible for external trade said during the election campaign. He said, and I quote:
No one is planning any changes in the unemployment insurance program. There hasn't been any change proposed to us since we dealt with the Forget Commission. We are not contemplating any changes.
That is from The Evening Telegram of St. John's, Newfoundland of October 14, 1988, page 3. Now it is quite clear to me that no changes were planned to the unemployment insurance program.
As it turned out there were changes planned which will have a profound effect in many areas of our country, in particular on the people of eastern Ontario who are so ably represented in this House by my distinguished colleagues sitting around me.
In the Ottawa area, according to Employment Insurance Canada, the unemployment rate is 5.7 per cent. At the present time one must work 14 weeks in order to receive 46 weeks of unemployment insurance.
April 25, 1989

Under the proposed system one would have to contribute 20 weeks in order to receive 35 weeks of benefit. That is in conflict with the promise made to us by the Minister for external trade.
However, it goes beyond that. The fact that this Government has broken a promise is something that we expect from these Tories, but I refuse to accept the unfairness of this system. Even if it were true that where unemployment is lower warrants a tightening up of unemployment insurance rules, and I am not even saying that that in itself is an acceptable way of doing things, it certainly is not true in the constituency that I represent.
In Hawkesbury, Ontario, in my riding, the unemployment rate is 12.6 per cent. In Cornwall, in the riding of Stormont-Dundas ably represented by my colleague, the unemployment rate is 11 per cent. In Pembroke, so ably represented again by my colleague from Renfrew, the unemployment rate is 9 per cent. That 9 per cent unemployment rate has factors in it such as those living closer to Ottawa. The point is that the people of my riding are being asked to receive less unemployment insurance benefits because they are allegedly living in an area of low unemployment. I have just demonstrated that such is not the case. Unemployment is very high in the constituency I represent.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration, in an answer to a question I raised in the House on April 17, said that her colleague, the Minister of State, "announced that we would be revising the boundaries for unemployment insurance and that they will recognize regional differences".
Part of that answer may be correct. However, my question was specific. I want to know whether those boundaries will be changed before the new rules are applied. I want an ironclad guarantee for my constituents, as well as the constituents of Stormont-Dundas, Renfrew and elsewhere in eastern Ontario, that those rules will not be changed, the ones pertaining to UIC benefits, until they redo the map. Otherwise people living areas of 12 per cent and 13 per cent unemployment, such as the one my colleagues and I represent, will be punished by this unfair measure of the Government.
Adjournment Debate
Today I am asking the Government to take this occasion to reassure my constituents about this very vital issue.

I can assure the Hon. Member that this study of regional boundaries is still taking place. I am positive it will be completed long before the legislation passes the House.
About 23 per cent of unemployment insurance beneficiaries reside in rural areas, traditionally characterized by high unemployment rates. The proposed changes do not impact on high unemployment regions, and rural centres will continue to receive the same protection under the unemployment insurance program.
Indeed, the proposal will not increase entrance requirements nor reduce benefit entitlement where unemployment is highest. Moreover, the proposal eliminates the repeater provision to make it easier for seasonal workers to qualify.
I also want to bring the attention of the Hon. Member to aspects of the Labour Force Development Strategy announced by the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration on April 11. The Hon. Minister then proposed, among other things, additional funding for human resource planning, business development centres in designated communities, as well as assisting displaced and older workers. CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON AGRICULTURAL WORKERS-SUPPLY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on April 4, in the House, I specifically asked the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) to set up programs which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had promised to Canadians during the election.
The Prime Minister said at that time: "I want to tell Canadians we shall ensure that innovative and generous adjustment and retraining programs will be introduced whenever and wherever required".
Quite frankly, the Hon. Minister did not answer my question. I cautioned those in the House on April 20, 1989, that the food conglomerates like Heinz and Nabisco were threatening reduction in their labour force caused by free trade. In fact, the Council of Canadians, in its third report card on the Free Trade Agreement, listed 26 companies with a possible loss of 7,619 jobs due to companies moving to the United States or being taken over by mergers with other companies.
One does not need much imagination to estimate the dire consequences and complete demolition of communities around which these companies are built and of employees which make up these companies.
The Deputy Prime Minister has refused to recognize what is happening and is completely ignoring the need for any of the "innovative and generous adjustment and retraining programs" promised by the Prime Minister. The time is now, not tomorrow, not next week or the week after, for the Government to bring in the programs that were promised during the election.
My supplementary question concerns the well organized supply management systems we have in Canada, which I stress duly comply with the GATT laws. Unfortunately, the Deputy Prime Minister and the de Grandpre report totally ignored the importance of supply management to Canadians and Canadian farmers.
I am of the opinion, which is supported by many supply managed industries, that we should not dismantle these effective and working organizations. The Deputy Prime Minister stated that de Grandpre fully endorsed the concept of supply management. That is just it. It is a concept. It is a form only.
In reality free trade undermines supply managed systems at every opportunity. By introducing an unworkable two-price proposal, de Grandpre continues to chip away at the supply managed industries.
According to the Canadian Dairy Commission, the two-price system would create an artificial incentive for highly processed products. If dairies made cream cheese, for instance, they would pay the regular price for milk. However, if they made pineapple flavoured cream cheese, they could claim to be engaged in further processing and pay the lower rate.
Furthermore, such a system would be a nightmare to monitor. It would be impossible to regulate the procedure that de Grandpre has introduced. We do not have enough people now to monitor our present inspection system without creating another one.
The Consumers' Association of Canada does not think very much of the two-price proposal either. It believes that the recommendations amount to protecting processors and producers by dipping into the consumers' pockets. The National Farmers Union observes that the proposals are an attempt to Americanize Canadian agriculture. The Chicken Marketing Board is doubtful if a two-price system would work.
The report urged the chicken, turkey and dairy boards to hold meetings within six months with provincial agencies and processors to discuss a two-price system. If the boards refuse to consider a two-price system, the Government should permit higher annual levels of imports to help the processors. Talk about holding a club over the heads of producers. That is what chicken producers feared from the free trade deal in the first place. In fact, there is already a lot of U.S. produced chicken moving into Saskatchewan and it has already depressed prices.
The Deputy Prime Minister went on to say that the fact of the matter is that the supply management service is in place, and that what we have to do as a Government and as an industry is to ensure that the systems are preserved and enhanced. This a flagrant dichotomy if there ever was one. The national and provincial farm organizations representing poultry producers strongly oppose free trade. The Ontario Chicken Producers' Marketing Board, the Tbrkey Producers' Marketing Board and the Ontario Egg Producers Marketing Board maintain that the national supply management programs have served producers, processors, government and consumers well. They do not support this attempt to attack the supply management system.
April 25, 1989

The Ontario Hatcheries Association also supports the maintenance of supply management. Marketing boards opposed to any changes in the present tariff and non-tariff barriers include asparagus producers, tender fruit producers and grape growers. All these groups have pointed out that Ontario is at a significant climatic disadvantage when competing with American states, not to mention the variance in operation costs, wages and employment benefits.
Our system is a good one. It is not only good but it is functional. When I asked the Deputy Prime Minister for his response, he said that he was considering the de Grandpre proposals. That is not good enough. Throughout the election campaign, we listened to the Deputy Prime Minister say that he would have programs available for farmers. To date, we have seen nothing.
A couple of weeks ago, I became the godfather of Michael Barilla, a person from Hagersville whom I would be proud to see grow up to be a farmer. I cannot ask him to do that today, particularly with a Government which is not prepared to help farmers.
I see that you are signalling that my time is up. Madam Speaker. I would like to end by saying that we on this side of the House are prepared to do something for farmers. We are prepared to stand up for farmers and we are prepared to propose policies that we feel will help the farming community.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON AGRICULTURAL WORKERS-SUPPLY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first like to thank the Hon. Member for Haldimand- Norfolk (Mr. Speller) for his concern regarding supply managed commodities under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. I would like to assure the Hon. Member that Canadian farmers will continue to benefit from supply management programs in the new trade environment.
The Hon. Member said that the Government has done nothing for farmers. I can proudly say that the Government has probably done more for agriculture than any Government in history that either I can remember or the Hon. Member can remember. We have done what we said we would do for agriculture.
Adjournment Debate
Under Article 710 of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, both countries maintain the rights outlined in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. These rights, which were reaffirmed just last week in Geneva, allow Canada to continue to operate domestic supply management systems.
In other words, we have retained our right to add products to the import control list if they threaten to undermine an industry operating under supply management. We have exercised this right. Since the agreement went into effect at the beginning of the year, the Government has expanded the import control list to include yoghurt, ice cream, and other dairy products, to ensure that our dairy markets are not disrupted.
The slight increase in import quotas for chicken, turkey, and eggs under Article 706 of the agreement should not be interpreted as a threat to the supply management programs operating for these commodities. The quota changes simply reflect actual imports required to meet domestic consumer demand over the past few years.
